  • Hide the base map and background on upper layer: Set the upper visual’s background to hidden under Display settings and disable the base map under Map options.
  • Stack the visuals: Move the top visual on top of the base layer using drag-and-drop or by matching precise size and position coordinates under Display settings.

Layer ordering follows the visual stacking order in the free-form layout. To change a visual’s position in the stack, choose the menu icon (three dots) on the visual, then choose Send backward or Bring forward. Readers can access the tooltip of the topmost visual, so place the layer that readers need details from on top. Each sheet supports up to five layer map visuals.

Dynamically updating GeoJSON

Unlike other Quick Sight visuals where data refreshes through SPICE or Direct Query, layer map geometry lives in the GeoJSON file itself. When your dataset refreshes on schedule, the metrics update (for example, colors change and tooltip values refresh), but the geometry remains at its original position.

To update what appears on the map, like a new route, new point locations, or updated boundaries, you need to update the GeoJSON file and republish the dashboard. You can replace a GeoJSON file manually through the Quick Sight console by editing the layer map visual within the Analysis and uploading a new file. This works for infrequent changes such as updating territory boundaries quarterly or adding a new store location.

For automated, on-demand, or dynamic updates, the process involves Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the Quick Sight APIs outlined in the following steps:

  • Upload the new GeoJSON to Amazon S3: Generate your updated geometry and save it to an Amazon S3 bucket. Custom solutions can use other AWS services such as Amazon Location Service to create the GeoJSON files.
  • Reference the file on the dashboard definition: The dashboard definition contains a StaticFiles array with a SpatialStaticFile entry for each GeoJSON file. Modify the file reference to the S3 location of your updated file entry for each GeoJSON file.
  • Call the UpdateDashboard API: Submit the updated definition with the new file reference using the UpdateDashboard API.
  • Call the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API: Publish the change so it is visible to dashboard readers with the UpdateDashboardPublishedVersion API.

The following example uses this pattern to support on-demand map updates in an embedded dashboard to generate optimal routes between locations and waypoints. Although outside the scope of this post, this represents an advanced use case that combines each of the preceding approaches.

Figure 9: On-demand route generation in an embedded dashboard

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how to use Point and LineString geometry in Amazon Quick Sight layer maps to plot specific locations and the routes between them. We covered the GeoJSON structure and dataset join that layer maps require, and compared layer map points with the native point map. We also walked through advanced techniques for controlling the viewport, layering separate visuals into one view, and refreshing GeoJSON files with Amazon S3 and the Quick Sight APIs.

To learn more about layered maps, refer to the Amazon Quick Sight layered maps documentation. Visit the Amazon Quick Community to connect with peers and stay updated on the newest features and resources.

About the authors

item.title: [Amazon Bedrock] How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on A…
item.description: Full title: How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

How Bayer Crop Science built an agentic decision engine on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with AWS Unified Operations

Plant breeding decisions depend on data that spans genomics, field trials, imagery, environmental conditions, and model outputs. Bayer Crop Science runs hundreds of machine learning (ML) model configurations against this data across crops, regions, and teams, and each run needs to be repeatable and governed. To meet that requirement, Bayer built the Connected Decision Engine (CDE), a system for deploying, orchestrating, monitoring, and reusing ML workflows. CDE gives breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and data engineers a consistent way to run analytics while preserving execution history and operational controls.

As adoption grew, the bottleneck moved from running workflows to understanding them. Explaining a result meant piecing together context from APIs, documentation, metadata stores, dashboards, and logs. A user who wanted to know why a workflow failed, what a model did, or where a result came from still had to know which system to inspect. To close that gap, Bayer built the Agentic Decision Engine (ADE), a multi-agent, natural language interface over CDE. A supervisor agent routes each question to a specialist agent, the specialist retrieves context from the relevant system, and the user receives an answer without navigating the operational stack. In its first phase, ADE resolves about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop.

ADE runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, an AWS service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. AgentCore let the team focus on agent behavior instead of building and operating its own agent hosting, session isolation, and tool access layer. Three AgentCore capabilities drove that choice: a managed runtime that isolates each user session, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped tool access through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, that keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code, and a framework-agnostic design that let the team bring its own LangGraph orchestration and choice of models.

To prepare for launch and to operate ADE afterward, Bayer engaged AWS Unified Operations. The engagement provided a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a generative AI Domain Specialist Engineer (DSE), who worked as an extension of the ADE team from design through production. The TAM, as Bayer’s strategic advisor, brought an established understanding of Bayer’s operating model and business priorities. The DSE brought generative AI domain expertise on AWS. In three technical standups each week, the team reviewed and made design decisions. The DSE built working knowledge of the ADE workload and how the Bayer team operates, so technical guidance reflected both AWS service behavior and Bayer’s context. This post follows that journey: the ADE architecture, five design decisions made during the build, the work to prepare the platform for production, and how it is operated after launch.

Architecture overview

ADE is organized into four layers: the user experience, agent orchestration, specialist agents, and the tools and data sources those agents call (Figure 1). Users reach ADE through a React web front end, and requests pass through an identity proxy for Microsoft Entra ID before they reach the agents. GitHub Actions builds the agent container images, pushes them to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and deploys them to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the agents, and because the runtime is framework-agnostic, the team runs its own LangGraph-based orchestration on it directly. The team chose LangGraph for its explicit graph-based control flow and checkpointing for multi-step workflows. LangGraph orchestrates the workflow, with a Supervisor Agent as the entry point that classifies each request, selects a specialist, and combines results when a question spans domains. The data plane is separated by responsibility. Amazon DynamoDB stores LangGraph checkpoint state. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL stores session records, user feedback, and analytics. Amazon ElastiCache caches agent responses with a time to live (TTL). Domain content in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) is embedded with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and indexed in Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG). Amazon CloudWatch captures runtime and application telemetry. AgentCore Gateway exposes backend APIs to agents as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and keeps authentication and authorization outside agent code.

Figure 1: Agentic Decision Engine architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore

ADE runs 22 specialist agents in production, each scoped to one domain with its own tools and data sources. For example, the Domain Expert Agent answers conceptual questions through RAG. The Operational Agent retrieves live workflow status and results from CDE. The Troubleshooting Agent analyzes operational telemetry. The Visualization Agent generates charts or returns existing dashboards. A customer-specific Models as Skill pattern converts model code and documentation into skill definitions stored in a central registry, so agents answer model-specific questions from the model’s implementation instead of generic model knowledge.

When a breeder asks, “Why did my phenotyping workflow fail yesterday?”, the supervisor classifies the intent and routes the request to the Troubleshooting Agent. That agent reads the workflow’s telemetry in CloudWatch and its status from the CDE API through AgentCore Gateway, identifies the failure point, and returns a diagnosis through the supervisor (Figure 2). The breeder doesn’t search logs directly. With the Troubleshooting Agent, a diagnosis that once took over an hour of manual log-hunting and waiting for engineer support now takes under 10 minutes.

Figure 2: ADE request flow: intent classification, cache lookup, specialist routing, and response

Five design decisions on the path to production

The Unified Operations TAM and DSE took part in the following decisions as members of the working team, not as an escalation point after the fact. That let Bayer test each design against AWS service behavior before committing to it, while keeping ownership of the architecture and the final call.

1. Externalize orchestration state without treating the runtime as stateless

AgentCore runtime provides isolated sessions that preserve execution context across invocations within a session’s lifecycle. That context isn’t a durable store for a multi-step workflow. ADE writes LangGraph checkpoints to DynamoDB so the graph can resume after scale-out events, restarts, or session boundaries without depending on one execution environment remaining available.

Principle: Use the runtime session for active execution, and persist the state required to resume or reconstruct the workflow in a durable service.

2. Separate enterprise identity, gateway access, and downstream authorization

Bayer standardizes on Microsoft Entra ID for user identity, while ADE’s services authorize each other with AWS-native mechanisms. Rather than force one token across every trust boundary, the team gave each boundary its own mechanism.

Entra ID remains the source of user identity. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) authorizes service-to-service calls. AgentCore Gateway outbound authorization handles access to downstream CDE services. A request interceptor AWS Lambda function performs custom validation and passes the authorization attributes that downstream tools require. The team worked through the token contract at each hop with the DSE.

Principle: Identity failures in agent systems cluster at the transitions between user identity, agent identity, and tool identity. Define the issuer, audience, claims, scopes, and credential lifetime at every hop instead of reusing a token that is valid for one boundary at the next.

3. Treat model selection as an interface contract

During the build, the team evaluated a newer model version with reasoning mode enabled. For that version, the combination of tool use and structured output that ADE depends on was not compatible with how its agents were implemented. The DSE confirmed the constraint, and the team retained the current model for the release.

Principle: For tool-using agents, model choice is constrained by the full interface: tool calling, structured output, streaming behavior, reasoning features, latency, quota availability, and model-specific request semantics. A newer model is not automatically a drop-in replacement.

4. Control the tool surface before it controls the prompt

CDE manages more than 500 model configurations. A dedicated MCP server per API would have added deployment, authentication, and version management overhead. ADE instead registers OpenAPI specifications with AgentCore Gateway, which exposes the REST operations as MCP tools. Adding or changing an API becomes a schema and gateway configuration change instead of a new server deployment.

Tool schemas and descriptions also consume input tokens and compete with the user’s request and retrieved context. ADE scopes tools by specialist agent instead of giving every agent the full catalog. For larger catalogs, AgentCore Gateway supports semantic tool search, so an agent can find relevant tools without loading the entire catalog on every turn.

Principle: Scope the tool catalog per agent. Every tool definition adds tokens and widens the model’s decision space.

5. Promote complex capabilities from tools to agents

Visualization started as a tool invoked by other agents. As it grew, it needed its own data retrieval, chart selection logic, retries, error handling, and a decision about whether to generate a chart or return an existing dashboard. The team moved it into a specialist Visualization Agent. The agent generates on-demand charts with matplotlib and Plotly in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides a sandboxed code execution environment, and exchanges data with it through Amazon S3. When a prebuilt dashboard is the better answer, the agent returns the existing Amazon Quick or Power BI asset.

Principle: A tool performs a bounded operation. When a capability starts to own state, retries, planning, policy, or presentation decisions, model it as an agent.

Preparing ADE for production

As the build moved toward launch, the focus shifted from design to operability: detecting agent failures, attributing inference cost, and hardening the deployment.

Observability: Measure task failures, not only exceptions

A supervisor architecture turns one user request into a chain of model calls, tool calls, and agent handoffs. The final answer can be wrong even when every HTTP request succeeded. ADE encountered this directly: application exception handlers caught agent errors and returned responses that monitoring counted as successful. After reproducing the issue with the DSE, the team added custom CloudWatch metrics inside failure paths and alarms on agent-specific conditions: tool call errors, throttling, model timeouts, and structured output validation failures. Traces and invocation logs follow each request across the supervisor and specialists.

Principle: Distinguish transport success from task success. Agent observability should show whether the task completed, which agent or tool changed the outcome, and whether the response used the expected source.

Cost attribution: Combine billing attribution with request-level telemetry

One ADE request can invoke several models and tools, so account-level Amazon Bedrock spend doesn’t explain unit economics. The team designed the attribution approach with the DSE using three mechanisms that answer different questions. Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles attribute billed model usage to an application or workload. Request metadata and model invocation logging associate token usage with a specific agent, feature, or request. IAM principal attribution adds an identity dimension. Together they let the team estimate cost per interaction, identify expensive agents, and determine whether prompts, retrieved context, or tool definitions drive token use. In practice, the Visualization and Operational agents, which rely on MCP tools and multiple tool calls, consumed the most tokens.

The same telemetry surfaced a workload during launch preparation with a large repeated input prefix and no prompt cache activity. For supported models, placing stable instructions and tool definitions in a cacheable prompt prefix reduces repeated input processing, which lowers latency and token cost. For ADE, caching the stable prompt prefix cut input-token cost by 20–30 percent.

Security and launch readiness

IAM roles are scoped to each agent’s responsibility. The Troubleshooting Agent can read the operational data it needs for diagnosis but can’t modify workflows. The Domain Expert Agent can query its retrieval index but cannot call unrelated CDE APIs. In production today, ADE’s agent responses are governed by least privilege, read-only tool access scoped to each agent, structured output validation on agent responses, and answers grounded in retrieved CDE data and telemetry rather than open-ended generation. Bayer also plans to evaluate Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as an additional layer on these controls, complementing the custom safety checks already used in CDE multi-turn workflows.

Before launch, Unified Operations ran a Critical Workload Review and a Well-Architected review with the Generative AI Lens alongside the ADE team. Because the DSE already knew the workload, both reviews targeted ADE’s specific failure modes, capacity risks, and deployment gaps rather than generic best practices. Findings included gaps in failure visibility across the supervisor and specialist agents, mutable container image tags, limited image traceability, and missing vulnerability scanning. The team responded with stronger alarms, immutable versioned images, scan on push in Amazon ECR, and lifecycle policies for unused images.

The DSE also reviewed scaling and quota requirements with the team. Load testing validated both the application and its service quotas and exposed a networking failure mode that returned empty responses, which the team fixed before the production event. By launch, the team had tracked 35 blockers to resolution with Unified Operations.

Launch, operations, and next steps

Bayer launched ADE to a gated group rather than opening it to the whole organization at once. Since launch, more than 100 users across Bayer Crop Science have used ADE, including breeders, analysts, researchers, data scientists, and engineers. Alongside its 22 specialist agents, ADE exposes about 20 API tools and can host third-party agents as it expands. Exposing those APIs through AgentCore Gateway rather than a dedicated server per API cut per-API integration overhead by more than 99 percent. In its first phase, ADE has resolved about 80 percent of user questions without an engineer in the loop.

CDE remains the governed execution layer for analytics. ADE adds a natural language layer over it, so users can ask about workflow status, results, model behavior, and failures without learning the location or interface of each underlying system.

The engagement then shifted from launch readiness to ongoing operations. The DSE continues to meet with the team, so issue triage and operational reviews start from existing knowledge of ADE instead of a new ramp-up. ADE’s critical CloudWatch alarms, including the agent-specific alarms described earlier, are onboarded to AWS Incident Detection and Response. When one fires, AWS Incident Management Engineers engage within 5 minutes and start from the workload’s context rather than from scratch. On the security side, AWS Security Incident Response engineers support the team during potential or active security events, so ADE has AWS monitoring and response coverage for both operational and security issues.

With agent-to-agent communication already in place, Bayer is focusing next on hybrid cloud agent interoperability. The team is exploring how agents running in different environments can discover and communicate with each other without manual configuration.

Conclusion

Bayer didn’t replace its analytics platform with ADE. It made CDE easier to query and operate. Most of the production work sat outside the prompts: durable state, identity boundaries, tool scoping, task-level observability, cost attribution, and launch readiness. Bayer owned the architecture and each of those decisions. Working with a designated DSE and TAM through AWS Unified Operations, the team tested those decisions against AWS service behavior during design and carried the same context into production.

To learn more, explore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Amazon Bedrock cost attribution, AWS Well-Architected Generative AI guidance, and AWS Unified Operations.

The authors would like to thank Sijie Shi, Jorge Gomes, Naveen Reddy, Iago Fonseca, Mateus Silva, and Sushimitha Jarugula for their contributions to the design, development, and launch of ADE.

About the authors

item.title: [DeepInfra] Best API Providers for Wan 3.0 Integration
item.content:encoded:
Best API Providers for Wan 3.0 Integration

Published on 2026.10.23 by DeepInfra

Wan3.0 is Alibaba’s all-in-one video generation model. It accepts text, images, video, audio, documents, and web pages, and it produces up to 30 seconds of 1080P video with synchronized audio.

Production use raises practical questions. Video jobs run asynchronously, reference inputs can be large, and each provider exposes a different slice of the model’s features and bills it differently.

This guide compares the main API providers and SaaS platforms for Wan3.0, with what each one actually charges. Match one to your integration, compliance needs, and budget.

Summary of the Best Wan3.0 Providers

Here is a quick summary of the platforms covered below:

ProviderBest for
DeepInfraTeams that want one API across several Wan generations and other video models, with zero data retention
Alibaba CloudEnterprise teams that want first-party access and regional pricing
Atlas CloudTeams that need SOC 2 Type II certification and HIPAA-aligned hosting
RunwareDevelopers who want first-frame, last-frame, and reference image control through one inference API
falWeb developers who want a typed JavaScript client with queue progress updates
PoYoDevelopers who prefer credit-based billing with credits that never expire
MuAPIDevelopers who want polling or webhook delivery and access to Standard, Prime, and Spicy variants

Detailed Provider Reviews

DeepInfra

DeepInfra hosts Wan-AI/Wan3.0-Video as an all-in-one endpoint. One model identifier covers reference-based generation, editing, replication, and driving, and the media array you send decides which workflow runs.

Key features

  • Media types for first_frame, last_frame, reference_image, reference_video, reference_audio, file, and link, all in one array
  • Controls for duration (2 to 30 seconds, or -1 for a model-chosen length), resolution, aspect ratio, audio, prompt extension, watermark, and seed
  • A JSON response with a video_url plus an inference_status object that reports status, runtime, and cost
  • A zero-retention policy for inputs, outputs, and user data, with SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification

Differentiators for Wan3.0

DeepInfra serves the Wan family from Wan2.2 through Wan3.0 behind one API, including Wan2.7 reference-to-video and Wan2.6 image-to-video. Teams can compare generations, or step down to a cheaper model for drafts, without changing vendors.

The same account also reaches other labs’ video models, such as ByteDance Seedance 2.0. A single integration can route between Wan3.0 and alternatives for an A/B test.

Pricing

Wan3.0-Video is billed at a single flat rate of $0.20 per second of generated video, with no separate charge by resolution. A 5-second clip costs $1.00, a 10-second clip costs $2.00, and a full 30-second generation costs $6.00.

Lighter Wan models stay on the same account at lower rates: Wan2.7 and Wan2.6 cost $0.10 per second, and Wan2.2-T2V-A14B costs $0.075 per second. Since Wan3.0’s flat rate equals Alibaba’s own 1080P price, it fits final renders better than low-resolution drafts, which cost less elsewhere.

Alibaba Cloud (Model Studio)

Alibaba Cloud is the creator of Wan3.0 and offers it through Model Studio under the model name wan3.0-video. A faster wan3.0-video-prime tier uses the same parameters and media rules.

Key features

  • Text, image, video, audio, file, and link inputs, with one document (up to 100MB or 50 pages) or one web link per request
  • Output at 480P, 720P, or 1080P, up to 30 seconds, with smart duration recommendation
  • Video editing that changes visuals, plot, or dialogue without regenerating the full clip
  • First-frame and first-and-last-frame image-to-video
  • A limit of 300 requests per minute in every listed region

Differentiators for Wan3.0

As the first-party host, Alibaba Cloud ships new Wan3.0 capabilities before any reseller, including editing and extension from the same generation API. The trade-off is a narrower feature set: no function calling, structured output, web search, prefix completion, context caching, batch inference, or fine-tuning for this model.

Pricing

Pricing is regional. Singapore lists $0.05, $0.10, and $0.20 per second at 480P, 720P, and 1080P. The US, Germany, Japan, and China regions list a flat $0.041256, $0.082513, and $0.165025, around 20% below Singapore at every tier.

The Prime tier costs more: Singapore lists $0.068, $0.14, and $0.28 per second, and the other regions list $0.0636, $0.127199, and $0.254399. These are listed as original prices and exclude any promotion. A separate comparison of DeepInfra and Alibaba pricing on a shared language model shows the same first-party-versus-reseller pattern.

Atlas Cloud

Atlas Cloud lists Wan 3.0 and Wan 3.0 Prime with text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video endpoints. It shares a unified key with its other Wan versions, so Wan 2.5, 2.6, and 2.7 users switch by changing only the model name.

Key features

  • Up to 20 mixed references per request: 10 images, 5 videos capped at 15 seconds total, and 5 audio clips capped at 15 seconds total
  • One document, up to 100MB or 50 pages, or one webpage through a deep thinking mode
  • Native audio on by default, and native duration up to 30 seconds with smart duration (-1)
  • SOC 2 Type II certification and HIPAA alignment

Differentiators for Wan3.0

Atlas Cloud pairs compliance listings with discounted rates rather than a published per-resolution breakdown. The bill runs lower alongside SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA documentation, and both instruction-based and reference-based editing match Alibaba’s own feature set.

Pricing

Wan 3.0 standard lists at $0.05 per second, shown at $0.04 after a 20% discount. Wan 3.0 Prime lists at $0.068 per second, shown at $0.061 after a 10% discount. Atlas Cloud does not publish a separate rate per resolution tier, so confirm the current per-second price against your target resolution before committing to volume.

Runware

Runware is an inference platform that exposes Wan3.0 under the model ID alibaba:wan@3.0. Its overview lists text-to-video, image-to-video, video-to-video, audio-to-video, edit, and extend modes behind that one identifier.

Key features

  • frameImages for a first frame, or a first and last frame for a morph, as a UUID, URL, data URI, or Base64 string
  • referenceImages for up to 10 images that guide subject or product identity without appearing in the output
  • referenceImages combinable with referenceVideos and referenceAudios in the same request
  • Resolutions of 480p, 720p, or 1080p, with 1080p as the default when none is set

Differentiators for Wan3.0

Runware’s schema keeps the controls explicit and catches mistakes before a job runs. frameImages and referenceImages are mutually exclusive, and sending both returns a validation error rather than an ambiguous result. width and height are rejected once an input image is attached, since only pure text-to-video takes explicit dimensions.

Pricing

Runware’s model reference for Wan3.0 does not publish a per-second or per-resolution rate on the page. Pricing is set through the account dashboard, so confirm the live rate there before estimating a monthly cost.

fal

fal is a generative media platform that serves Wan 3.0 and Wan 3.0 Prime through the alibaba/wan-3.0 and alibaba/wan-3.0-prime endpoints. Its parameter set stays close to Alibaba’s own API.

Key features

  • A JavaScript client published as @fal-ai/client, with queue progress callbacks and a request ID on every call
  • enable_prompt_expansion, on by default; turning it off can save roughly 20 to 60 seconds of latency at some cost to quality
  • enable_thinking for enhanced reasoning before generation, off by default
  • enable_safety_checker, on by default; disabling it requires account authorization, and unauthorized requests are checked regardless

Differentiators for Wan3.0

fal’s queue-based client returns a request ID immediately and reports progress through onQueueUpdate. This suits browser applications that show generation status rather than block on one long request. The thinking and safety-checker toggles give finer control over latency and moderation than most resellers expose.

Pricing

Standard pricing is $0.05, $0.10, and $0.20 per second at 480p, 720p, and 1080p, the same as Alibaba’s Singapore rate. Prime pricing is $0.068, $0.14, and $0.28 per second. A 5-second 720p Prime clip costs $0.70. fal notes that pricing is subject to change.

PoYo

PoYo is an API platform that bills in credits rather than a metered per-second rate. Its Wan 3.0 card lists 10 credits per call, and credits never expire once purchased.

Key features

  • Text-to-video, first and last frame control, and multimodal references in one API
  • Reference inputs that include images, video, audio, documents, and links
  • Videos up to 30 seconds
  • A separate Wan 3.0 Video Prime tier at 13.6 credits per call, with optional generated audio

Differentiators for Wan3.0

Credit billing gives teams a fixed number to budget against before each call, rather than a rate that scales silently with resolution or duration. Developers who prefer prepaid balances over metered invoices will find the model simple to track. The trade-off is that PoYo does not expose a per-second cost comparable to the other providers here.

Pricing

Wan 3.0 costs 10 credits per generation, and Wan 3.0 Video Prime costs 13.6 credits per generation. PoYo does not publish a per-second rate, so the per-video cost depends on the credit package you buy rather than on resolution or duration.

MuAPI

MuAPI offers Wan 3.0 as Standard, Prime, and Spicy variants. Each variant covers text-to-video, image-to-video, and reference-to-video, with endpoints such as wan3.0-text-to-video and wan3.0-prime-text-to-video.

Key features

  • A REST API with an x-api-key header that returns a request ID
  • Results by polling the prediction result endpoint, or by a webhook_url that notifies you when the video is ready
  • Reference-to-video with up to 10 images, 5 videos, and 5 audio clips, the same limits for Standard and Prime
  • thinking_mode for complex or multi-step prompts, and a Wan 3.0 node pack for ComfyUI

Differentiators for Wan3.0

MuAPI gives backend teams a choice between polling and webhook delivery, which matters for workers that cannot hold an open connection for a multi-minute generation. The Spicy variant produces higher-contrast, higher-motion output from the same three workflows, and the ComfyUI node pack extends that choice to visual pipelines.

Pricing

Prime is billed by resolution and duration, from $0.136 per generation at 720p and 2 seconds up to $8.40 at 1080p and 30 seconds. The per-second math matches fal and Atlas Cloud Prime: $0.068, $0.14, and $0.28. Standard and Spicy are pay-per-second, with the exact rate shown in the completed task response.

Conclusion and Recommendations

Integrating Wan3.0 means weighing your infrastructure, compliance needs, and developer tooling against each provider’s pricing. The per-second rate alone does not tell the whole story.

  • Enterprise and compliance: Atlas Cloud lists SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA alignment at a discount. Alibaba Cloud offers first-party access with regional pricing and the earliest access to new features.
  • Workflow control: Runware’s explicit frame and reference schema suits pipelines that mix first frames, reference images, video, and audio. Confirm pricing in the dashboard, since the model page does not list it.
  • Web development: fal’s JavaScript client, queue updates, and separate thinking and safety-checker toggles suit browser-based products that need visible generation status.
  • Budgeting and delivery options: PoYo’s credits simplify spend tracking before each call. MuAPI supports polling or webhooks, with Standard, Prime, and Spicy variants at matching per-second Prime rates.

DeepInfra is a strong default when you want one API across Wan generations, zero data retention, and a single listed rate for 1080P renders. A similar guide covers the SaaS tools and API platforms for Kimi K3.

Related articles

GLM-5.1 on DeepInfra: Z.AI’s Agentic Engineering Model<p>Z.AI’s GLM-5.1 scores 58.4 on SWE-Bench Pro — ahead of both Claude Opus 4.6 (57.3) and GPT-5.4 (57.7) on real-world software engineering tasks. It’s the direct successor to GLM-5, designed for agentic engineering: long-horizon coding tasks, terminal operations, and repository-level work. The core design premise is that previous models, including GLM-5, tend to plateau after […]</p>

Wan 3.0 API Benchmarks: Speed, Latency & Cost<p>Key Takeaways Wan is Alibaba’s family of video generation models. The earlier Wan2.2 models ship as open weights under Apache 2.0, while later releases such as Wan2.6, Wan2.7, and Wan3.0 are delivered through hosted APIs. Wan 3.0 is the first Wan model to accept documents and web pages as input. It also doubles the maximum […]</p>

From Screenshots to Tool Calls: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on DeepInfraNVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, the new open multimodal model in the Nemotron family, is available on DeepInfra from day zero. It brings visual understanding, reasoning, and tool calling together in one model, through an OpenAI-compatible API with pay-per-token pricing.

item.title: [Inference.net] Introducing AutoEvals: Automatically find the best model for…
item.description: Full title: Introducing AutoEvals: Automatically find the best model for your task
item.content:encoded:
Aug 5, 2026

Introducing AutoEvals: Automatically find the best model for your task

A

Amar Singh

It's the Summer of 2026. A new frontier model is released nearly every month. Each one comes with a new set of benchmark numbers, some hype on X, and the same nagging question for teams running LLMs in production: should we switch?

Most teams never really answer it. Answering it honestly means building a dataset that represents your real traffic, standing up API access to every provider you want to test, writing a rubric, wiring up judging infrastructure, burning the tokens to run it all, and then interpreting the results. That's a week of work, per model, per task, every time something new ships. So the question gets shelved. The model that was chosen months ago, based on a price point and vibes, keeps running because swapping models in production is both hard and risky.

And the risk is real. Benchmarks are averages over someone else's tasks. A model can top the leaderboards and still fumble your tool schemas, your output format, your edge cases. The only benchmark that actually matters is your own traffic, and until now, nobody had time to run it.

We're introducing tooling to fix this. Introducing AutoEvals - the plug-and-play toolkit to find the right model for your task. Sign in or read the docs to get started.

Real production traffic is the best benchmark

AutoEvals is designed to help developers find the best model for a given task or agent. Not the best on a public benchmark you never heard of - better on the exact requests your users sent last week.

Integrate with Inference Gateway (in 2 minutes), collect data, click one button in the dashboard, and a few minutes later you have a definitive answer about which model you should use, with real numbers on the difference in quality, cost, and latency.

Every model release becomes free upside instead of homework. When something new ships, you no longer weigh the announcement against a week of eval work. Run a comparison over lunch and know by the afternoon whether it matters for you.

Switching stops being scary. The recommendation isn't a leaderboard rank. It's your own traffic, replayed and judged, with every sample inspectable. You can understand exactly how a new model handles requests compared to your current model before a single production request touches it.

You stop paying for intelligence you don't need. Plenty of tasks are quietly overserved by expensive models. AutoEvals shows you the quality-cost frontier for your specific task, so you can see when a more affordable model offers the same level accuracy.

The verdict: a concrete recommendation for your task, with the reasoning behind it

How AutoEvals work in practice

An AutoEval runs in three moves. It starts by sampling your recent production traffic, which is then replayed by a set of candidate models. Afterwards, LLM judges score each output for both quality, meaning how well the model did the task, and similarity, meaning how closely it behaves like the model you run today. It then summarizes these results into a model verdict, key findings, and per-model summaries.

The two scores together tell you how safe a switch is. High quality with high similarity is a drop-in upgrade. High quality with low similarity means the model is good but behaves differently, so it earns a closer look first. When you do want to inspect the outputs individually, the Sample Viewer gives you side-by-side model responses and the judge's reasoning for each score.

The Sample Viewer: side-by-side model responses and the judge's reasoning for each score

Getting your traffic in front of Inference platform is the only setup, and it's one integration: route your LLM calls through our Gateway (our CLI can instrument your project automatically), or report traces with our tracing SDK. From then on, comparing models is a button, and switching is a single line change.

Running on our own agents

We built AutoEvals for our own agents before we built it for anyone else, and two findings genuinely changed how we think about model selection.

The gap between model generations is bigger than you think. One of our GTM agents had been running on the same well-regarded model for months. It felt fine, until we ran an AutoEval on it. Models at a fraction of the cost blew it out of the water with better long-horizon trajectories, tighter tool-schema adherence, and more precise results across the board. We left better results on the table because we didn't look.

Some tasks have a skill ceiling. On that same task, the top frontier models landed on identical quality scores. Past a certain capability level, they were all simply taking the right action, and paying more bought nothing. Once you can see the ceiling, the model decision makes itself, and it's rarely the most expensive option.

Past a certain capability level, quality converges - paying more buys nothing

Put those two findings together and the conclusion is hard to escape: if you're building with LLMs, your application should be getting more accurate and cheaper over time, just from the pace of model releases. The teams that capture that compounding advantage will be the ones for whom evaluation is effortless. That's what we built.

Run your first comparison today

AutoEvals are live now for every Inference account, free to start. Connect your traffic, click Run Comparison, and in a few minutes you'll know something most teams never find out: whether the model you're running is actually the best one for the job.

Read the guide or sign up free to get started.

The best model for your task might have shipped last week. Now you can actually find out.

CONTACT

Meet with our research team

Schedule a call with our research team to learn more about how Specialized Language Models can cut costs and improve performance.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent…
item.description: Full title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve built an agent in Claude Platform that includes multiple subagents, see which may make sense to fold into the main agent loop using our migration kit. It runs a guided workflow to identify your patterns, evaluate alternatives, and verify the best approach. It includes a demo that you can try on a mock system before running on your agent.

Subagents – agents with their own context window, tools, and instructions, orchestrated by a coordinator – are a core component of agent design. They are effective at verification, parallel work, and modular permissioning. We use them in many of our own agents that we build using Claude Platform, for example our multi-agent research system.

However, recently the Applied AI team has found a pattern of enterprise agent deployments that have benefited from folding routers, planners, and domain subagents into the main agent loop. In our comparisons across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, and often at a lower cost and latency per task.

For example, one company found the dozen of specialist subagents within its customer-facing agent made a consistent on-brand experience difficult to maintain and added latency that hurt the user experience.

We also often see proposed agent designs that follow a familiar progression: an intent classifier, a fixed multi-step reasoning pipeline, user-segment buckets, separate recommendation branches, and a multi-agent orchestrator on top.

In these cases feedback is often that most of this structure was doing work the model no longer needed done for it, and that one clear system prompt, 4-5 thin data tools, and firm output guardrails would cover most of the use case.

To be clear, subagents still have their place, including at the research frontier. Use them when:

  • A single agent loop hits measurable performance degradation from context bloat, or
  • Multiple tasks need to be tackled in parallel with fresh context windows that can be discarded once the task is done, or
  • A single agent struggles to select appropriate tools or there are conflicting instructions in the system prompt.

But too often we see enterprises give each team or problem type its own subagent, with the agent architecture becoming a copy of their org chart (Conway’s law at work).

This post explains when to consider folding subagents into your main agent loop with best practices we’ve learned from building agents in large organizations.

Agent building failure modes for large organizations

Companies often want to build an agent that unites multiple products and capabilities into a single customer interface.

Typically, each capability is owned by a separate team, so companies start by letting each individual team build their own agent, then a central platform team builds an orchestrator on top. This can take on several structures including orchestrator-subagent or a single agent with specific agents exposed as MCP tools.

This looks like the simplest solution but introduces immediate complexity around:

  • Context management: You need to decide what context is exchanged between agents and often lose details in the back and forth.
  • Subagent sprawl: Every team ships its own subagent, so companies end up with hundreds of overlapping subagents with no enforced standards and no specific owner.
  • The Frankenprompt: Every team adds a sentence to the system prompt, resulting in conflicting rules and no consistent voice.
  • Unvetted, overly localized evals: Everyone adds their own evals that are overly optimized for their subtask. No one owns or maintains the whole set, and leadership makes decisions based on watered-down, overly localized scores.
  • Latency: Multi-agent architectural complexity adds latency. One customer that evaluated their multi-agent harness against a single agent loop saw a roughly 2x faster runtime with the latter.

Using an agent loop with progressive disclosure

The orchestrator-subagent design described above is a reasonable approach to coordinating specialists built across teams, but often a more effective approach can be progressively disclosing context via skills and progressively disclosing tools via tool search. In other words, the agent sees short descriptions of the skills and tools, which are fully loaded only when needed.

There are three reasons why this approach can make sense:

  • Shared context produces better answers: for longer-running agents, we want the context from several different tasks to sit in the main context window. An agent that has seen the result of each earlier step can connect them, which leads to richer outputs and better insights than a set of summaries handed back by subagents. It also means fewer context windows and fewer lossy handoffs.
  • Progressive disclosure prevents context bloat: this technique allows teams to build single agents that can accomplish a wide variety of tasks without requiring all of the context to be immediately loaded into one long system prompt. This removes the main reason teams previously split work across subagents. In fact, we reduced Claude Code’s system prompt for more advanced models by over 80% which included cuts related to progressively disclosing skills and tools.
  • Models are more capable: starting with Opus 4.5, models became capable of managing far more in a single loop than most teams expected. You cannot turn off thinking on Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.1, and recent models increasingly narrate their progress and check their work as they go, which makes some harness elements redundant. Each new model lets you move more of the decision-making out of the harness and into the model itself. A simpler loop is also easier to move to the next model; in migrations we have helped customers with, rigid multi-agent structures were often what stopped the new model from doing more of the work.

The single agent loop design requires discipline: a carefully managed system prompt, skill and tool descriptions that trigger at the right times, and deliberate handling of context windows, memory, and note-taking. This article goes deeper into migration and design considerations in subsequent sections.

One central team should own end-to-end quality and the system prompt, vetting every new tool and eval before it ships. Keeping that central team small helps iteration move quickly and lowers coordination cost across a large org.

If you go the multi-agent route, start with the simplest pattern (generator-verifier, orchestrator-subagent, or other) that could work. Decompose boundaries effectively by dividing by context: give each subagent a piece of work that needs little from the rest of the system and have it hand back a compact result (good candidates are independent research paths, separate components with clean interfaces, or black-box verification). When agents are split by problem type, they engage in a "telephone game," passing information back and forth with each handoff degrading fidelity.

How to fold subagents into the main agent loop

Many teams already have an orchestrator and a set of specialist agents in production. The following is the single loop design we'd suggest working toward:

  • One model and one context window running an open-ended tool loop, with limits (turn and cost budgets, write gates) set in the harness.
  • Each turn, the model emits a batch of tool calls. The harness runs them in parallel and returns raw results to the same model, which decides the next step: another batch, a question to the user, or an answer.
  • The loop stops when the model answers or hits a budget. A goal or verifier check can optionally run after the answer.
  • The model writes its plan in context on the first turn and revises it as results arrive. This is the main change from the orchestrator and specialist agents setup: the model that writes the plan is also the one carrying it out, so it can change the plan mid-turn.
  • Context still gets loaded, and is managed by the agent itself:A code step that rewrites the plan from a catalog of rules is no longer needed, since the model decides each step.Ordering and domain procedure move into skills.Hard limits (validation, approval gates) and anything else that comes up mid-conversation (e.g. memory lookup) move into the tools.Code can still be used to load anything cheap and almost always relevant (e.g. an entity resolution step), and to handle any mechanical parts (payload construction, stream parsing, resuming a clarification) inside tools the loop calls.

This single loop design also helps with the end state many teams are working toward (an agent that understands a user's high-level goals and acts on their behalf), since it keeps everything the agent has learned in one context.

The suggestions below are how a team could get from a multi-agent system to a single agent loop in stages, and how several teams can keep contributing to that agent along the way.

Task-completion evals

The first step is to create an eval set that can help you determine whether you should fold a subagent into the main agent loop. The eval structure we’ve seen work is one shared end-to-end set owned by a central team with smaller eval sets shipped with each skill by the team that owns it. Even a set of 10 golden examples is enough to start.

Grading the agent's final message against a rubric is a good starting point for tracking answer quality. While you still have an orchestrator, you should also track routing accuracy (did it pick the right subagent?). Once a subagent is folded in, check instead whether the agent loaded the right skill or called the right tool. Working toward task-completion evals over time is helpful as this matters most when comparing architectures.

This can be complex in environments where internal systems are difficult to replay and user engagement is difficult to simulate. One approach that has worked for us internally is to record timestamps on important events, so they can be replayed later to run as targeted evals.

Reducing subagents over time

Evolving toward a single agent loop involves folding the subagents into tools and skills. This can be done by merging domain subagents, calling them as tools, or replacing them with skills and tools.

Combining domain agents

Build a small end-to-end eval before the first merge. Then fold in by shared context starting with subagents that have the most use.

Merge specialists that chain on each other's output, touch the same data, or are often called together. For example, if a significant share of production traffic is one specialist followed by a second, that is a tightly coupled pair, which makes it a candidate to merge into one domain agent.

Subagents called as tools

When one of the three conditions above applies and you keep a subagent, it can be effective to have the main agent call subagents as tools so it can continue holding the conversation with the user.

We’d only recommend a full handoff, where the subagent takes over the conversation, when it needs to talk to the user directly. Everything else can be a skill plus tools in the main loop.

This will allow you to define a shared response schema for subagents, verify the conclusion against real data with the main agent, and trim the input to any final synthesis step. This is a good first step, as you don’t need to rewrite the subagents. It also gives you a baseline on the task-completion eval before deciding to fold any subagents into the main agent.

However, some failure modes will remain:

  • Each specialist has its own prompt, context, owner team, and evals
  • Each call still hands back a lossy summary
  • Every call is a nested model loop that adds latency

Folding subagents into the main agent via skills and tools

Fold subagents into the main agent one at a time by turning each one’s prompts into skills and API calls into MCP tools. Compare eval performance with and without the subagent. Then decide which to keep.

When you compare, don’t just examine the final score, take a look at which tasks flipped. When we tested this on a sample support agent, folding one subagent into another lowered latency, but also broke a process that had been passing. The main agent was holding the order lookup tool and answering on its own, without asking the shipping specialist for the delivery date.

Before each change, make sure your eval has a task for every chain of agents that runs together in production and for every rule the agent must not break, and run each task more than once, since a break like this one only showed up in one run out of two.

How several teams can contribute to a single agent

Domain reasoning can be retrieved from knowledge bases, skills, and MCP tools. Individual teams can shift their ownership from agents to skills and tools, with one small central team keeping ownership of the system prompt and end-to-end quality. This involves vetting new skills, tools, and evals before they ship.

MCP tools

Tools are the right fit when the agent needs to take an action, read live data from a system, or return a result in a fixed shape. You can also use tools as a way to keep calling subagents while you migrate. We recommend tools grouped by user intent (not one tool per API) because once you exceed 30-50 tool definitions in the system prompt, tool choice tends to degrade.

Use tool search with deferred loading, limit hard preconditions, and move any needed ones into the tools. For example, if Y needs X's output, Y's tool checks for it and returns an instruction the model can act on. Per-user permissions work the same way. Each tool checks what the calling user may see or do and returns a plain refusal the model can read, so one loop can serve users with different access without a separate agent per permission level.

Skills

Skills are the right fit when the agent needs to know how a team does work, like the steps, rules, and judgment calls a specialist subagent's prompt used to hold.

Our approach to growing skill libraries is to give the maintenance work back to the people writing the skills. Claude can do the heavy lifting with skills that can build, test, and prune other skills.

To prevent skill sprawl, you can have DRIs per team own their skills and make sure they are well crafted, distinct, and shipped with appropriate evals.

  • /skill-creator allows you to author new skills that start well-formed, and audit existing ones to trim, deduplicate, and restructure them.
  • /skill-doctor allows you to see what each skill in your library costs and how often it’s actually used, and delete dead weight.

Knowledge bases

Knowledge bases are the right fit for reference material the agent only needs some of the time. Facts and reference material (policies, metric definitions, product specs) can sit behind a search or lookup tool the model calls, or ship as reference files inside a skill. Avoid having code retrieve and paste this context into prompts.

Tools to accelerate this work

We recently released a set of Claude API skills that can help with most of the work mentioned above. Our migration kit chains these skills together in one guided workflow for assessing and moving multi-agent systems to a single agent loop. It includes a demo you can try before running it on the real thing:

  • /claude-api build-eval: can help create a first end-to-end set owned by the central team or small evals each team ships with its skill
  • /claude-api prompt-audit: can flag instructions written for older models in your prompts, skills, and tool descriptions and propose fixes as a diff. This can be run on your system prompts to find any rules that were added for an earlier model and are now making the agent slower or more rigid. Each team's DRI can also run it on their own skills and tool descriptions.
  • /claude-api hillclimb: can iteratively improve an app against an existing eval. This can be used for the "folded in vs kept" comparison (after folding one subagent into a skill plus tools, let it iterate on the skill and tool descriptions and see if the folded version matches or beats the subagent), as well as your system prompt.
  • /claude-api cost-optimize: profiles where your calls go and proposes savings from options such as prompt caching, trimming unneeded input and output tokens, effort, and model choice, one change at a time. This can help bring cost and latency down on a given design.

As models evolve, our understanding of how to best use them and guidance around best practice evolve as well. That makes any one architecture less important than the principle behind it: measure, change one thing at a time, and keep what holds up.

This is one of those cases. As models get more capable and agents get longer running, more of your subagents can be skills and tools. You don’t have to make that move in one step, though. Build a small end-to-end eval, fold in one subagent, and keep it as a subagent only if the folded version scores worse, then rinse and repeat.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] The full Claude Platform, available on Google Cloud
item.content:encoded:
Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is now generally available, giving Google Cloud customers the full set of Claude Platform features, with Google Cloud IAM credentials, billing, and commitment retirement. Claude also remains available via the Google managed offering, where Google is the data processor.

Access the complete Claude Platform on Google Cloud

With the Anthropic managed offering, Google Cloud customers now receive the full set of Claude API features, with new features and betas shipping the same day they go live on the native Claude Platform.

The Anthropic managed offering works with existing Google Cloud IAM credentials, so teams can stay within the tools and permissions they already manage. Billing is through a single Google Cloud invoice and Claude usage draws down your existing Google Cloud commitment.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is currently available with US and Global endpoints.

“With the Anthropic managed offering, we get the native Claude API with Google Cloud as the access layer. Accessing new features on day one is important. We build AI agents and assistants for Enterprises, and need to bring new Claude capabilities into our product quickly. Using our existing IAM set-up and knowing usage counts towards our Google Cloud commitment made it an easy decision for our team.”

Arvind Sundararajan, CTO

“Moby, our AI harness for ecommerce brands, runs on Claude. With the Anthropic managed offering, we run Moby on Google Cloud on the same Claude API our team already builds on. Prompt caching is central to how we run Moby cost-effectively at scale, and we’ve kept it while running billing and access through Google Cloud.”

Maksim Gorev, Head of AI Engineering

What’s included

Google Cloud customers using the Anthropic managed offering get the full set of Claude Platform features, so they can:

Build and deploy agents with:

  • Claude Managed Agents (beta) (opens in new tab) to power long-running agents, without managing infrastructure
  • Code execution (opens in new tab) to run Python code, create visualizations, and analyze data within an API call
  • Computer use (opens in new tab) to allow Claude to operate a browser or desktop to complete tasks
  • Agent skills (opens in new tab) to teach Claude repeatable workflows so it delivers consistent results
  • Advisor strategy (beta) (opens in new tab) to give agents an intelligence boost by consulting an advisor model

Connect to systems and knowledge with:

  • Files API (opens in new tab) for uploading and referencing documents across conversations
  • Citations (opens in new tab) for grounding responses in source documents
  • Web search (opens in new tab) and web fetch (opens in new tab) to augment Claude’s knowledge with current, real-world data from across the web
  • MCP connector (beta) (opens in new tab) to connect Claude to other tools without writing client code

Manage cost and performance with:

  • Prompt caching (opens in new tab) for reducing costs and latency on repeated context
  • Batch processing (opens in new tab) for high-volume, asynchronous workloads

Fast Mode on Claude Opus 5.5 is also generally available for customers using Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Fast mode prioritizes speed, offering up to 2.5x faster output token generation, for rapid iteration, live debugging, and interactive agents where output speed results in a better user experience. Input and output tokens are $8 and $40 per million.

See the full list of features available on Claude Models on Google Cloud in our documentation (opens in new tab).

Customers using the Anthropic managed offering also get access to the Claude Console, Anthropic’s development environment for observing and managing agents with Claude. The Console includes tools to write prompts and configure agents, run them on hosted environments, monitor usage and costs, and manage access and security per workspace.

Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are available, with new models shipping on the Anthropic managed offering as they launch.

Two paths to build with Claude

There are two ways to build with Claude on Google Cloud.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) is built for customers who want day zero access to all beta and generally available Claude Platform features. It’s best for customers who want full Claude Platform feature parity, accessed through Google Cloud. Anthropic operates the service and acts as the data processor.

Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed) remains the best choice for customers who need Google Cloud as the data processor, have strict regional data residency requirements, or want native Google Cloud integrations like Model Armor or Agent Engine.

Get started

The Anthropic managed offering is generally available today. To get started, open Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed) (opens in new tab) or explore the documentation (opens in new tab).

If you have an existing discount, please contact your Anthropic or Google Cloud account executive before getting started with the Anthropic managed offering, to ensure your discounts are applied correctly. Discounts cannot be applied retroactively to usage.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.

Agent interoperability through simplicity

A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.

Donating Agent Skills to AAIF

We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.

We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.

Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.

What comes next

We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.

Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

item.title: [Anthropic Claude] Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.

You can submit a proposal for a project here.

Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.

We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.

We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.

We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.

We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.

Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.

This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.
