item.description: Full title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

Team Article

Published October 21, 2026

15

Bernardo França de Aguiar

bernardoaguiar

Dharma-AI

Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso

GabrielPimenta99

Dharma-AI

Bruno Duarte

brunoduarte01

Dharma-AI

Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves

falves9101

Dharma-AI

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

A Vocabulary Built for Everyone

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Why Existing Solutions Fell Short

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

How We Solved It

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

What Changed in the Grader

To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Beyond the Grader

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Sources

  • Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2022).
  • Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023).
  • Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. "In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026).

Further Reading

  • Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order
  • GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft
  • Why Specialization Is Inevitable
  • Specialization Beats Scale: A Strategic Variable Most AI Procurement Decisions Overlook
  • Text Degeneration: A Production Failure Mode That Most Benchmarks Do Not Track

item.title: [Hugging Face] Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AW…
item.description: Full title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

Enterprise Article

Published October 21, 2026

7

Josh Longenecker

jlongen-aws

amazon

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:

  • How to configure torch.profiler with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace.
  • How to read the key_averages() table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time.
  • How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore.
  • How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation.

Neuron as a PyTorch Backend

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

Set Up the Profiler

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:

  • NeuronConfig controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it to torch.profiler.profile as experimental_config.
  • NeuronProfiler takes a NeuronConfig and provides an export_trace callback. The callback writes the framework trace, trace.json, alongside the Neuron system traces.
nc = NeuronConfig(
    modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
    profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
    capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
    correlate_device_time=True,
)
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Tooling: Neuron Explorer

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

Profile RMSNorm

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:

  • Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply.
  • torch.rms_norm(), the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.
  • Naive RMSNorm with torch.compile, using the same operations as the first implementation.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

device = torch.device('neuron')

x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    x_sq = t * t                                    # square
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)       # mean of squares
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)               # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps)
    return t * rms * weight                         # normalize + scale

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:

  • Include ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1 to collect activity from the Neuron device.
  • Pass NeuronConfig as experimental_config to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

with torch.profiler.profile(
    activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
    experimental_config=nc,
    record_shapes=False,
    on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace,
    schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
    for step in range(4):
        with torch.no_grad():
            _ = rms_norm_fn(x)
        torch.neuron.synchronize()
        prof.step()

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
aten::mul360.9 μs1,164.5 μs49.5%
aten::add126.6 μs434.6 μs18.5%
aten::rsqrt115.6 μs415.0 μs17.6%
aten::mean121.1 μs340.8 μs14.5%

Self NEURON total: 2.355 ms

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x x, x rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Read the Trace in Explorer

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

LaneLabel suffixWhat it shows
Framework dispatchframework/TID:<id>Operator dispatch events (PrivateUse1 runtime), grouped by thread ID.
Framework deviceframework/Stream:<n>Device interaction events (PrivateUse1 driver), grouped by stream number.
Neuron Runtimeneuron_rt/NC:<n>Neuron Runtime API calls, grouped by logical NeuronCore.
Neuron Hardwareneuron_hw/NC<n>:<id>Hardware execution events, grouped by physical NeuronCore.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Profile 2: torch.rms_norm

Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:

def rms_norm_fn(t):
    return torch.rms_norm(t, [512], weight)

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
aten::_fused_rms_norm147.6 μs403.3 μs100%

Self NEURON total: 403.3 μs

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

Compare the Lowering Path

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

@torch.compile(backend='neuron', fullgraph=True)
def naive_compiled(t):
    x_sq = t * t
    mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
    rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
    return t * rms * weight

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

Name# CallsSelf CPUSelf NEURON% NEURON
Torch-Compiled Region: 0/0198.4 μs375.5 μs100%

Self NEURON total: 375.5 μs

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Side-by-Side Summary

VariantNEURON timeSelf CPU timeOperator calls
Naive ops2,355 µs~125 µs6
torch.rms_norm403 µs~48 µs1
Naive + torch.compile376 µs~98 µs1

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Conclusion

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

item.description: Full title: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster

Enterprise Article

Published October 21, 2026

16

George Saon

gsaon

ibm-granite

Brian Kingsbury

bedkingsbury

ibm-granite

Ron Hoory

rhoory

ibm-granite

Vishal Sunder

vishalsunder

ibm-granite

Zvi Kons

konszvi

ibm-granite

Jeff Kuo

ibm-jeffkuo

ibm-granite

Samuel Thomas

sthomas12

ibm-granite

Avihu Dekel

Avihu

ibm-granite

Hagai Aronowitz

hagaia

ibm-granite

Takashi Fukuda

fukuda1

ibm-granite

Tohru Nagano

tohru3

ibm-granite

Sashi Novitasari

sasnov

ibm-granite

Masayuki Suzuki

szuk

ibm-granite

Madison Lee

kristunlee

ibm-granite

We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said.

ModelStatusWhat's newBest for
granite-speech-5.0-2bNewMore accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translationHigh-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation
granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctcUpdatedMultilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverbHigh-throughput and on-device transcription
granite-speech-4.1-2b-plusUpdatedImproved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performanceMeetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings

Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control

granite-speech-5.0-2b is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation.

What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech:

  • More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
  • Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription.
  • Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences.
  • Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language.
  • Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets.

The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon.

Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets.

Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster

When we introduced Turbo CTC in August, it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most:

  • Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
  • Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step.
  • More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings.

It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level.

Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale.

Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when

The updated granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas:

  • Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall.
  • Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review.
  • Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%.
  • Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists.
CapabilityMetricPrevious releaseUpdated model
Timestamps, all speechAAS (average timestamp shift)210.8698.54
Timestamps, short speechAAS (average timestamp shift)29.2726.20
Keyword biasingBiased-word WER, 20-term lists11.796.48
Long-form speechWER, long-form test sets13.5310.22
Speaker attributionWDER4.404.10
Speaker-attributed transcriptscpWER30.5028.48

Table 1: All metrics are error rates, so lower is better. For more detailed results, see the model card.

Get started

Not sure which model to pick? Start here:

  • Need high transcription accuracy, translation, or keyword biasing? Use granite-speech-5.0-2b.
  • Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc, and try it in the browser with our WebGPU streaming demo.
  • Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus.

These models are all released under an Apache 2.0 license with native support in Transformers. Full evaluation results, architecture details, training data, and usage examples are on each model card. We recommend pairing them with Granite Guardian for production deployments that need additional risk detection.

Give them a try and let us know what you think!

item.description: Full title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required

Enterprise + Article

Published October 21, 2026

6

Joshua Przybylko

jprzybylko

nvidia

Jure Leskovec

profjure

nvidia

Matthias Fey

rusty1s

nvidia

Federico Lopez

flopeznv

nvidia

Valter Hudovernik

valterh-nv

nvidia

Akihiro Nitta

akihironitta-nv

nvidia

Ramona Bendias

RBendiasN

nvidia

Ardrian Wong

aw777

nvidia

TL;DR

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers up to 10,000 historical examples as context and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models library or as an NVIDIA NIM.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview

The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models

Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.

The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:

Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.

Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.

Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.

Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational (paper, documentation), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.

How Kumo Relational Works

Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.

Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning, reading up to 10,000 context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").

![Overview of the NVIDIA Kumo Relational system: (a) database integration, (b) a prompting interface that turns natural language into a predictive query, and (c) automatic context generation feeding the NVIDIA Kumo Relational model, which scales horizontally across tenants.]

Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.

To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:

![Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input with task, users, orders and items tables; (b) column and row attention within tables with injected context targets; (c) graph attention and cross-sample attention across tables.]

Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.

Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.

Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently, alternating column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.

Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, interleaved with cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.

How Kumo Relational Was Built

Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.

The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. Members of the Kumo team helped develop PluRel and co-authored the original paper. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited, and the PluRel paper shows that pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.

Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. When maximum accuracy matters, Kumo Relational can also be fine-tuned on a specific dataset and task.

Performance

In this paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. On the RelArena-α leaderboard, which compares relational models and systems on RelBench V1, it also sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front out of the box:

![Scatter plot of the RelArena-α leaderboard: relative accuracy as Elo across tasks (y-axis) versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (x-axis, log scale). Kumo Relational sits on the Pareto front at about 17 seconds and Elo 1,842. The highest-scoring entry, rt-plurel, reaches Elo 1,878 at about 7,300 seconds, roughly 430 times slower. Every other foundation model, feature-engineering system, and supervised model scores lower and runs slower than Kumo Relational.]

Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard: Elo across tasks versus median inference time per 1,000 samples (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than the highest-scoring entry at similar accuracy.

The paper also reports that on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR) and recent tabular foundation models by about 25%, and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when many noisy columns are added.

Limitations

Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions, which used at most 10,000 context examples in our benchmarks. Fine-tuning of the foundation model is designed for exactly this case. Predictive signals must also be reachable within a limited number of hops, so start with a focused query over a few relevant tables and expand the graph as needed.

Demo

Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through a custom graph engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. It is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular. The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The code below passes context examples, prediction entities, and their related tables to the model:

# pip install structured-data-models
import sdm

model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")
pred = model(
    # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
    x_context=...,
    y_context=...,
    # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
    x_query=...,
    # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
    related_context_tables=...,
    related_query_tables=...,
)

See the library's relational examples for complete RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines, including how to sample each entity's related tables.

To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request:

# pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]'
import sdm_client

client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url="http://localhost:8001")  # NIM URL
query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery(
    # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL):
    "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id",
    # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred):
    {"users": ..., "orders": ...},
)
pred = client.predict(
    # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict:
    query.materialize(indices=[1, 2, 3]),
    model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(),
)

See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks.

Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational

NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper, explore the quickstart notebook, or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here.

  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596
  • Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview
  • Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models/
  • Client code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client
  • Client PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/structured-data-models-client/
  • Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational
  • Quickstart notebook: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client/blob/main/examples/local/relational.ipynb
  • Related Research: Predictive Query Language (PQL), PluRel, Kumo Tabular

Acknowledgements

We thank the entire Kumo team for their invaluable support. Special thanks go to Josh Przybylko, Adi Wadaskar, Hema Raghavan, Manush Murali, Raja Rao DV, Keti Jovanovska, Zack Drach, Vanja Josifovski, Myungwhan Kim, Blaž Stojanovič, Siyang Xie, Alan Krumholz, Effy Fang, Abdullah Al-chihabi, Disha Dubey, Devan Johnson, Joseph Oliveira, Angela Liu, Miha Pelko, Vedaant Jain, Sally Liu, Aleksandar S. Sokolovski, Alex Porter, and Ramona Bendias.

More from this author

item.description: Full title: Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink
item.content:encoded:
Artificial Intelligence

Securing Quick access from corporate networks with AWS PrivateLink

When enterprise data sits behind a corporate firewall or in a private on-premises data center, there’s no direct network path from AWS, even though the AI agents and dashboards in Amazon Quick can query virtually any data source. Administrators must make sure their sensitive enterprise data isn’t exposed to the public internet while being accessible for AI-driven insights and actions.

For many enterprises, routing traffic over the public internet introduces unacceptable risk. Regulatory frameworks such as HIPAA, FedRAMP, and PCI-DSS often mandate that sensitive data remain within controlled network boundaries. Even where compliance isn’t the primary driver, exposing internal data paths increases the attack surface, complicates audit trails and introduces variable latency that can degrade the user experience.

This walkthrough shows you how to connect on-premises data sources to Amazon Quick privately, without traffic traversing the public internet. It assumes you already have AWS Direct Connect or an AWS Site-to-Site VPN linking your on-premises environment to your virtual private cloud (VPC). From that foundation, we configure VPC endpoints powered by AWS PrivateLink so that Quick can reach your private resources over the AWS backbone, then layer security groups and VPC endpoint policies for defense in depth.

By the end, you will have a network architecture that keeps traffic between Quick and your on-premises data sources off the public internet, reducing the attack surface, providing consistent low-latency connectivity, and giving you a clear audit trail for compliance.

Amazon Quick and establishing private network connectivity

Amazon Quick is an AI-powered workspace that brings search, analytics, research, and automation into a single conversational experience. Understanding which components reach your private network, and how, determines the architecture in the sections that follow.

Data access in Amazon Quick falls into two paths. User-facing traffic covers anyone opening the Quick console, interacting with a dashboard, making an API call, or using Quick Desktop. All this routes through VPC endpoints (see VPC endpoints for user and API access), keeping user sessions off the public internet.

Data-fetching traffic is when Quick itself reaches into your network to pull data. This is handled by VPC connections (see VPC connections for data source access), and it’s where most of the architectural decisions lie. The features and integrations that initiate data-fetching connections are:

  • Amazon Quick Sight queries on-premises databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, and others) directly through ENIs placed in your VPC. This is the heaviest consumer of VPC connections.
  • Amazon Quick Flows and Amazon Quick Automate are separate automation features. Flows handle repeatable tasks. Automate handles complex, multi-system orchestration with human-in-the-loop. Both invoke action connectors, including MCP servers hosted privately in your VPC. Any workflow that calls an internal API routes through this path.
  • Quick Agents underpin all conversational interactions and can invoke action connectors directly. When a custom agent calls a privately hosted MCP server or internal API, traffic flows through the VPC connection.
  • Amazon Quick Index builds a unified search layer across connected sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). For data inside your VPC or on premises, knowledge base VPC connections are currently supported only for Amazon Redshift. Sources such as Confluence, SharePoint, Box, Google Drive, OneDrive, and Amazon S3 can’t use a Quick VPC connection today (see Supported VPC data sources). You can still restrict Amazon S3 bucket access to a VPC endpoint through a bucket policy, which is a separate mechanism.
  • Amazon Quick Research accesses enterprise sources behind the firewall alongside public internet data for its citation-backed reports, using the VPC connection when reaching private sources.
  • Apps in Quick build interactive web applications on top of structured data and action connectors, inheriting the same VPC connectivity as Quick Sight and Flows.
  • Quick Spaces organize content from the preceding features but don’t initiate their own data connections.

These two traffic paths require two distinct private connectivity mechanisms that work together:

  • VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink): Handle user-facing traffic such as accessing the Quick website, making API calls, and administrative access. These keep user traffic off the public internet.
  • VPC connections: Handle data source traffic. Amazon Quick reaches into your VPC (and by extension, your on-premises network) to fetch data from databases, Amazon Redshift knowledge base sources, and internal APIs. These are configured within the Quick console.

Configuring private connectivity

This section walks through the four building blocks in order: VPC endpoints for user and API access, VPC connections for data source access, VPC endpoints for AWS data services, and outbound access to required external domains.

Prerequisites

Before configuring private connectivity for Quick, make sure the following are in place:

  • An active AWS account with an Amazon Quick Enterprise subscription (VPC connections require Enterprise edition).
  • An existing VPC in the AWS Region where Quick is deployed.
  • A supported AWS Region. Quick website VPC endpoints are not available in the AWS China Regions or the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.
  • An AWS Direct Connect connection or Site-to-Site VPN established between your on-premises network and your VPC. This is the private path that carries traffic from your data center into AWS.
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create and manage VPC endpoints, security groups, and Quick administration. To create VPC connections, the administrator’s IAM identity also needs quicksight:CreateVPCConnection, quicksight:DescribeVPCConnection, quicksight:ListVPCConnections, quicksight:UpdateVPCConnection, quicksight:DeleteVPCConnection, ec2:DescribeSubnets, ec2:DescribeVpcs, ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups, iam:ListRoles, and iam:PassRole scoped to the VPC connection execution role.
  • Access to your organization’s DNS management (Route 53 private hosted zones or on-premises DNS forwarders), as private DNS resolution routes traffic through VPC endpoints rather than public addresses.

VPC endpoints for user and API access (AWS PrivateLink)

VPC endpoints powered by PrivateLink handle all user-facing traffic to Amazon Quick, including the website, API calls, and embedded content. They prevent users from needing to traverse the public internet to access the Amazon Quick console.

Figure 1: Private access to Amazon Quick from a corporate data center through a VPC endpoint

As shown in Figure 1: (1) a client on the corporate network sends a request to Quick; (2) the request travels over AWS Direct Connect, through the Direct Connect gateway, into your VPC; (3) the Quick VPC endpoint evaluates the endpoint policy and allows or denies the request; (4) allowed requests reach Amazon Quick over the AWS network.

Planning your VPC endpoint architecture

When planning your endpoint architecture, begin by identifying the AWS Region where your Quick account is deployed, as VPC endpoints must be in the same Region. Choose subnets across multiple Availability Zones for endpoint ENI placement, and make sure those subnets have routes to your on-premises network through Direct Connect or VPN.

Design security groups that restrict traffic on the endpoint ENIs to only required ports and source ranges. If you want all traffic routed privately (including the calls Amazon Quick makes to Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, and Amazon Athena), plan VPC endpoints for those services as well (see Configuring data source VPC endpoints).

Creating VPC endpoints for Quick

Quick requires two interface VPC endpoints for full private access:

  • Website access endpoint – Service name com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight-website. This handles the bulk of user traffic to the Quick console. Private DNS names for the Quick website differ from the public URL, so you must create an A record for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com pointing to the VPC endpoint.
  • API access endpoint – Service name com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight. This handles programmatic API calls. When private DNS is enabled, existing API calls to quicksight.<region>.amazonaws.com automatically route through the VPC endpoint with no additional DNS configuration. For FIPS compliance, use com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight-fips.
Note: Not every Quick API is available through the API VPC endpoint. The following 13 APIs are not supported: the action connector APIs (CreateActionConnector, DeleteActionConnector, DescribeActionConnector, DescribeActionConnectorPermissions, ListActionConnectors, SearchActionConnectors, UpdateActionConnector, UpdateActionConnectorPermissions) and the flow APIs (GetFlowMetadata, GetFlowPermissions, ListFlows, SearchFlows, UpdateFlowPermissions). Automation that manages action connectors or flows programmatically needs a path to the public API endpoint. See Quick and interface VPC endpoints.

If administrators sign in to Amazon Quick as IAM users through the VPC, also create the AWS Management Console endpoints:

  • com.amazonaws.<region>.console.
  • com.amazonaws.<region>.signin.

To create the website endpoint in the Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) console:

  • Open the Amazon VPC console. In the navigation pane, under PrivateLink and Lattice, choose Endpoints, then choose Create endpoint.
  • Enter a Name tag (for example, my-quicksight-vpc-endpoint) and, for Type, choose AWS services.
  • Under Services, search for com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight and select com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight-website (Figure 2).

Figure 2: Naming the endpoint and selecting the Quick website endpoint service

  • Under Network settings, select your VPC. Under Additional settings, keep Enable private DNS name selected.
  • Select subnets in at least two Availability Zones, then select the security group for the endpoint ENIs (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Selecting the VPC, private DNS, subnets, and security group for the endpoint

  • Choose a Policy (see the following Setting up VPC endpoint policies section), add tags, and choose Create endpoint (Figure 4).

Figure 4: Choosing the endpoint policy and creating the endpoint

  • Repeat these steps for the API endpoint, com.amazonaws.<region>.quicksight.

Configuring DNS resolution

For the website endpoint, create an A record for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com and point it to the VPC endpoint DNS name. This way, when users on your corporate network resolve the Quick URL, traffic routes through the private endpoint rather than the public internet. For the API endpoint, enabling private DNS on the VPC endpoint is sufficient, as API calls automatically resolve to the endpoint’s private IP addresses.

A Route 53 private hosted zone only answers queries from inside the VPCs associated with it. Because your users connect from the corporate network, configure your on-premises DNS servers to forward queries for <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in the VPC (or host an equivalent record in your on-premises DNS). Finally, validate DNS resolution from your corporate network to confirm that requests resolve to private IPs within your VPC rather than public addresses.

To create the record in Route 53:

  • In the Route 53 console, choose Hosted zones, then Create hosted zone.
  • For Domain name, enter <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com (for example, us-east-1.quicksight.aws.amazon.com). Scoping the zone to your Region avoids overriding other Quick host names. Choose Private hosted zone, associate your VPC, and choose Create hosted zone (Figure 5).

Figure 5: Creating a private hosted zone in Amazon Route 53

  • In the new hosted zone, choose Create record (Figure 6).

Figure 6: Creating a record in the new private hosted zone

  • Leave Record name blank, choose record type A, turn on Alias, choose Alias to VPC endpoint, select your Region and the website endpoint’s DNS name, and choose Create records (Figure 7).

Figure 7: Creating an alias A record that points to the Quick website VPC endpoint

Setting up VPC endpoint policies

VPC endpoint policies restrict which accounts or organizations can use the endpoint. For Quick, policies can be scoped by AWS account ID or Organization ID. To change a policy, open the endpoint in the Amazon VPC console, choose the Policy tab, and choose Edit Policy (Figure 8).

Important limitation: For the Quick website endpoint, the Principal, Action, and Resource fields must all be set to *. Conditions might only be specified against the aws:PrincipalAccount or aws:OrgId attributes. More restrictive action-level policies are only supported on the API endpoint.

Website endpoint policy example:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": "*",
            "Resource": "*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:PrincipalAccount": ["012345678901"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

Figure 8: Opening the endpoint policy from the VPC endpoint details page

API endpoint policy example (restricted to specific actions):

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": "*",
            "Action": [
                "quicksight:DescribeUser",
                "quicksight:ListUsers"
            ],
            "Resource": "*",
            "Condition": {
                "StringEquals": {
                    "aws:PrincipalAccount": ["012345678901"]
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

Figure 9: Editing a custom VPC endpoint policy

VPC connections for data source access

While VPC endpoints handle user-facing traffic, VPC connections handle the server-side path, meaning Amazon Quick reaches into your VPC to access databases, Amazon Redshift knowledge base sources, and internal APIs.

How VPC connections work

Amazon Quick Enterprise edition is fully integrated with Amazon VPC. When you create a VPC connection in Amazon Quick, you are adding elastic network interfaces (ENIs) into your VPC subnets. These ENIs allow Quick to exchange network traffic with resources within your VPC and, by extension, anything reachable from that VPC, including on-premises systems connected through Direct Connect or VPN.

All standard VPC security controls apply to this traffic. Route tables, network ACLs, subnets, and security groups govern traffic to and from Quick in the same way they govern traffic between any other instances in your VPC. This means you can connect to:

  • Private databases not exposed to the public internet.
  • On-premises data sources reachable through Direct Connect or VPN.
  • Internal APIs accessible by IP address within your network.

Create a dedicated security group (for example, QuickSight-VPC) for the VPC connection ENIs. On each data source’s security group, allow inbound traffic on the database port from that security group ID.

Note for VPC connections created before April 27, 2023: The security group attached to the Quick network interface is not stateful. You must add an inbound rule that explicitly allows return traffic from your data source’s security group on all ports (0–65535), because return packets use randomly allocated destination ports. Connections created after that date use standard stateful behavior. See Security groups: inbound and outbound rules.

Creating the execution role

Amazon Quick doesn’t create the VPC connection execution role for you. Before you add the connection, create a dedicated IAM role (recommended), or update an existing role that already trusts Quick, such as aws-quicksight-service-role-v0 used in the screenshots in this post. The role needs:

  • A permissions policy that grants the Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) actions Quick uses to manage its ENIs (Figure 10).
  • A trust policy that allows quicksight.amazonaws.com to assume the role. Only roles with this trust policy appear in the Execution role list in the Quick console.

Permissions policy:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "ec2:CreateNetworkInterface",
                "ec2:DeleteNetworkInterface",
                "ec2:ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute",
                "ec2:DescribeSubnets",
                "ec2:DescribeSecurityGroups"
            ],
            "Resource": "*"
        }
    ]
}

Figure 10: Adding the Amazon EC2 permissions required by the VPC connection execution role

Trust policy:

{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Principal": { "Service": "quicksight.amazonaws.com" },
            "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
        }
    ]
}

Configuring a VPC connection

To create a VPC connection in the Quick console:

  • Sign in to Amazon Quick as an administrator. Choose your profile icon in the upper-right, then choose Manage account (Figure 11). If you don’t see this option, you’re not a Quick administrator.

Figure 11: Opening Manage account from the Quick profile menu

  • In the navigation pane, under Security, choose Manage VPC connections (Figure 12), then choose Add VPC connection.

Figure 12: Manage VPC connections under Security on the Manage account page

  • Provide the following (Figure 13): A descriptive VPC connection name. The VPC ID of the target VPC. This can’t be changed later. The Execution role you created in the previous step. At least two subnets in different Availability Zones. At least one security group ID. (Optional) If your database host name must be resolved through private DNS, enter the IP addresses of your Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints under DNS resolver endpoints.
  • Choose ADD.

Figure 13: Adding a VPC connection in the Quick console

The connection status shows UNAVAILABLE until Quick finishes provisioning the ENIs, then changes to AVAILABLE. A status of PARTIALLY AVAILABLE means one of the ENIs is unavailable, but the connection can still be used.

Configuring data source VPC endpoints

VPC endpoints (PrivateLink, used here for AWS service APIs) and VPC connections (Quick ENIs placed in your VPC; see VPC connections for data source access) are different mechanisms. Quick accesses other AWS services (Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon Athena, AWS Secrets Manager) when retrieving data for dashboards and analytics. If you want all traffic to remain private, including the calls Amazon Quick makes to these AWS services, create interface or gateway VPC endpoints for each:

ServiceEndpoint typeService name
Amazon S3Gatewaycom.amazonaws.<region>.s3
Amazon RedshiftInterfacecom.amazonaws.<region>.redshift
Amazon Athena*Interfacecom.amazonaws.<region>.athena
AWS Secrets ManagerInterfacecom.amazonaws.<region>.secretsmanager
AWS GlueInterfacecom.amazonaws.<region>.glue

** Athena isn’t supported as a VPC connection data source. The Athena endpoint keeps Athena API traffic on AWS PrivateLink only.*

Create these endpoints in the same VPC where the Amazon Quick ENIs are placed. Make sure route tables and security groups allow traffic between the Amazon Quick subnets and the endpoint subnets.

Enabling access to required external domains

While data traffic between Quick and your on-premises sources stays on the private network, users’ browsers still need to reach a set of domains for sign-in, static assets, client-side metrics, and integrations. Even with VPC endpoints configured, domains without VPC endpoint support need outbound connectivity, typically through your corporate proxy or firewall. If your account uses IAM Identity Center, browser sign-in also requires the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints (see Secure user access and identity federation).

Required external domains

DomainPurposeVPC endpoint support
<region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.comBulk of Quick website trafficYes
quicksight.<region>.amazonaws.comQuick public API callsYes
signin.aws.amazon.comAWS console sign-in for accounts that use IAM identitiesYes
<region>.signin.awsSign-inNo
*.cloudfront.netStatic assets (CSS, JavaScript)No
*.s3.<region>.amazonaws.comReports and thumbnailsYes
*.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.comClient-side metricsNo
*.kinesisvideo.amazonaws.comLive streaming of automation workflowsNo
apis.google.com/js/api.jsGoogle Drive file pickerN/A
*.officeapps.live.comQuick side panel extensionN/A
outlook.cloud.microsoftQuick side panel extensionN/A
*.sharepoint.comQuick side panel extensionN/A
*.office.comQuick side panel extensionN/A
*.office365.comQuick side panel extensionN/A

Source: Domains accessed by Quick.

Configuration guidance:

  • For domains with VPC endpoint support (the Quick website and API, signin.aws.amazon.com, and Amazon S3), create the corresponding VPC endpoints and DNS records.
  • For domains without VPC endpoint support, allow them through your corporate internet egress (outbound proxy or firewall). If user traffic egresses through your VPC, use a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
  • If your security posture requires URL-level filtering, use an outbound proxy or AWS Network Firewall domain filtering rules to allow only the domains listed earlier.
  • Test from a corporate workstation (or an instance in the same egress path): nslookup and curl against each domain confirm DNS resolution and routing.

Enforcing VPC endpoint restrictions

After your endpoints are configured and tested, you can enforce that all access to your Quick account must come through the VPC endpoint, blocking general internet access entirely. As a result, users can only reach Quick from your corporate network through the private path you’ve established.

Quick provides IP and VPC endpoint restriction controls that limit account access to a predefined list of IP ranges, VPC IDs, or VPC endpoint IDs. For example, you can create a rule that allows access only from the VPC endpoint used for Direct Connect, meaning anyone attempting to reach Quick from the public internet will be denied.

To configure through the Quick console (only administrators signed in with IAM credentials can access the restrictions page):

  • Choose your profile icon, then Manage account. Under Security, choose Manage IP/VPC restrictions.
  • In the Restriction field, enter the VPC endpoint ID (for example, vpce-001122def), enter a Description, and choose Add (Figure 14).
  • Choose Save changes to apply the rule.
  • Turn on Enforce restrictions.

Figure 14: Adding a VPC endpoint rule on the IP and VPC endpoint restrictions page

Alternatively, configure through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

aws quicksight update-ip-restriction \
--aws-account-id ACCOUNT_ID \
--region REGION \
--enabled \
--vpc-endpoint-id-restriction-rule-map \
vpce-001122def=CorporateVpcEndpoint
Note: UpdateIpRestriction replaces the entire rule map. Retrieve your current rules with aws quicksight describe-ip-restriction and include any existing rules in the update.

Key considerations:

  • IP and VPC endpoint rules apply to Quick web, embedded, and mobile access, meaning they don’t restrict access to the public API. To restrict API calls from specific sources, use IAM policies with aws:SourceIp or aws:SourceVpce conditions.
  • Make sure your own IP or VPC endpoint is included in the rules before enabling restrictions, otherwise you will lock yourself out.
  • Rules can take up to 10 minutes to take full effect.
  • You can combine IP rules and VPC endpoint rules, such that traffic is allowed if it satisfies either rule type. You can add up to 100 IP and VPC endpoint rules combined.
  • IP and VPC endpoint rules are enforced across all AWS Regions for your account, but you can only add or manage them from the AWS Region where your Quick account was created.
  • If you have publicly embedded dashboards, they will only be accessible through the VPC endpoint once restrictions are enabled.

After you enforce the restrictions, only traffic arriving through the specified VPC endpoint (or allowed IP ranges) can reach your Quick account. All other access is denied.

Secure user access and identity federation

Private network connectivity keeps traffic off the public internet, but it doesn’t answer the question of who can access what within Quick. This section covers how to integrate your corporate identity provider, control user provisioning, and enforce fine-grained access segmentation across Quick components.

Integrating with AWS IAM Identity Center

Important: For Quick accounts integrated with IAM Identity Center, browser-based authentication requires access to the public AWS sign-in and IAM Identity Center endpoints. VPC endpoints don’t provide this browser sign-in path. Public IP addresses aren’t required. Provide outbound connectivity through a NAT gateway or proxy. See Considerations for private access in the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

Amazon Quick uses AWS IAM Identity Center as the central point for workforce identity management. IAM Identity Center connects to your existing corporate identity provider (IdP) using SAML 2.0 for authentication and SCIM 2.0 for automatic user and group provisioning. This provides:

  • Automatic user provisioning and deprovisioning synced from your IdP.
  • Group membership synchronization – when a user is added to or removed from a group, that change propagates to Quick.
  • Single sign-on (SSO) using existing corporate credentials.
  • Temporary credentials through assumed IAM roles – no long-lived Quick-specific passwords.

For a step-by-step guide on setting up IAM Identity Center with your identity provider, see Getting started with IAM Identity Center.

Role-based access in Quick

Quick supports three base roles that determine what a user can do:

  • Admin – Full management access including data source configuration, VPC connections, security settings, user management, and SPICE capacity purchasing.
  • Author – Can create and publish dashboards, build agents, configure Spaces, manage data sources, create flows, and build apps.
  • Reader – Can view published dashboards, interact with agents, use Spaces they’ve been granted access to, and consume Quick Research reports.

These roles are mapped to IAM roles that federated users assume at sign-in. By managing role assignment in your IdP, you maintain a single source of truth for who has what level of access.

Additionally, Quick supports custom permissions profiles that can override default role permissions at the account, role, or user level. User-level permissions override role-level, which in turn override account-level. This gives administrators granular control beyond the three base roles.

User segmentation with Spaces

Quick Spaces provide an additional layer of access segmentation beyond roles. Each Space can be configured with specific user and group permissions, meaning:

  • A finance team Space containing sensitive revenue dashboards and financial knowledge bases is only accessible to the finance group.
  • A sales team Space with CRM-connected agents and pipeline dashboards is restricted to sales users.
  • Cross-functional Spaces can be shared across multiple groups with appropriate permissions.

Space-level access is controlled by the groups synced from your identity provider, so adding a new team member to the appropriate group automatically grants them access to the relevant Spaces.

Row-level security in Quick Sight

For dashboards backed by structured data, Quick Sight supports row-level security (RLS) that restricts which data rows each user or group can see. RLS is configured through dataset rules, which are a permissions dataset that maps users or groups to the field values they can access.

For example, a regional sales dashboard can be configured so that:

  • The EMEA sales group only sees rows where region = 'EMEA'.
  • The NA sales group only sees rows where region = 'NA'.
  • The VP of Sales sees all rows.

RLS rules are evaluated based on the user’s identity as determined by IAM Identity Center, meaning the same identity federation that controls sign-in also governs data-level access. This applies equally to traditional dashboard views and AI-powered natural language queries. The same security policies restrict what data the AI can reference when generating answers.

Column-level security

In addition to row-level restrictions, Quick Sight supports column-level security (CLS) to hide sensitive columns from specific users or groups. For example, a dataset containing employee information might restrict the salary and SSN columns to only the HR group, while other groups can still access non-sensitive columns in the same dataset.

How identity ties to private connectivity

The identity layer and network layer work together:

  • A user on the corporate network authenticates through your IdP → IAM Identity Center → Quick.
  • Their request reaches Quick through the VPC endpoint (the private network path; see VPC endpoints for user and API access).
  • Quick evaluates their identity to determine role, Space access, and RLS/CLS policies.
  • When Quick fetches data from an on-premises source, it uses the VPC connection (ENIs in your VPC; see VPC connections for data source access) to reach the database over Direct Connect.
  • The response is returned to the user through the same private path.

Apart from the sign-in and static-asset traffic described under Enabling access to required external domains, no traffic traverses the public internet, and at every point the user’s identity determines what they can see and do.

Validation and testing

Before enforcing restrictions in production, validate end-to-end connectivity for each access pattern:

Access patternTestExpected result
Website (VPC endpoint)nslookup <region>.quicksight.aws.amazon.com from the corporate networkResolves to a private IP in your VPC CIDR
Website (auth)Navigate to the Quick console from a corporate machineSign-in completes via IdP. Console loads normally
API (VPC endpoint)aws quicksight describe-account-settings from within the VPCReturns account settings; Flow Logs show source IP from your VPC
Data source (VPC connection)Create a test Quick Sight data source pointing to an on-premises database through the VPC connectionConnection test succeeds. Test query returns data
Knowledge base (VPC connection)Create a knowledge base from an Amazon Redshift source using the VPC connection, then trigger a syncSync completes. Content appears in the knowledge base
Action connector (VPC connection)Create a test action pointing to an internal API and invoke it through an agentAction returns the expected response
Embedded dashboardsLoad an embedded Quick Sight dashboard from an internal appDashboard renders. Browser dev tools confirm private IP

Monitoring

For ongoing visibility, enable VPC Flow Logs on all endpoint and VPC connection ENIs to capture traffic metadata. Monitor CloudWatch metrics on VPC endpoints (ActiveConnections, BytesProcessed, PacketsDropped) and set alarms for connection failures or unexpected traffic sources. These logs also serve as the audit trail referenced in your compliance documentation.
