The diagram shows a planned pipeline bringing information from Impact Manager, NetSuite, Salesforce, Paylocity, ThriveLink, and iQpay through Boomi into Amazon Redshift. Scheduled SPICE jobs then supply the data to Quick.

The next step for U.S. Hunger is to explore how its hunger data could become a national resource for researchers, the public, and companies. Rick has asked AWS for help shaping that work. The ambition extends the role of technology beyond internal analysis: Knowledge gathered while helping families could support research and generate revenue to help feed more families.

Conclusion

U.S. Hunger’s goal remains to feed families today and unite them to a healthier tomorrow. Direct data exploration, shared executive context, research, and financial analysis help its leaders understand both the organization they run and the families at the center of its mission.

Watch the video

Hear more from Rick Whitted in episode 8 of the Quick-witted podcast, “From Silos to Solutions.” He discusses how U.S. Hunger uses Amazon Quick and the role technology plays in its mission.

Learn more about U.S. Hunger and explore Amazon Quick capabilities and customer stories.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Granite 4.2 8B: Model Overview & Integration Guide
item.content:encoded:
Granite 4.2 8B: Model Overview & Integration Guide

Published on 2026.10.21 by DeepInfra

Granite 4.2 8B is an 8-billion-parameter dense transformer reasoning model developed by IBM. As the mid-size member of the Granite 4.2 family, it balances reasoning depth with operational efficiency.

Released under the Apache 2.0 license, the model is built for complex reasoning, code generation, tool calling, and structured data output.

Its defining feature is native chain-of-thought reasoning. Granite 4.2 8B performs step-by-step logical processing inside <think>…</think> tags before producing a final answer.

This supports applications that need deep logic, such as mathematical problem solving, agentic workflows, and software engineering tasks.

Capabilities and Performance

Native Reasoning and Flexible Thinking Modes

To give developers control over latency and computational depth, the model supports three thinking modes that can be toggled on a per-query basis:

  • Full Thinking (default): maximizes reasoning depth for complex queries and generates comprehensive chain-of-thought tokens
  • Low-Effort Thinking: provides brief reasoning for simpler queries, reducing time to first token
  • Non-Thinking: disables the reasoning phase entirely for the lowest possible latency

Benchmarks

The model has been tested across reasoning, knowledge, instruction following, and coding tasks:

CategoryBenchmarkScoreMetric
ReasoningAIME 202586.67Accuracy
ReasoningGPQA64.14Accuracy
KnowledgeMMLU-Pro74.04Accuracy
Instruction FollowingArena-Hard-V265.19Score
CodingSWE-Bench Verified47.67Resolved Issues

Compared to Granite 4.2 3B, the 8B variant offers greater reasoning depth. Compared to the 30B flagship, it remains more resource-efficient, making it a middle option for enterprise deployments.

Context Window and Multilingual Support

Granite 4.2 8B natively supports a 128K token context window, extendable to 512K tokens for long-context tasks.

This makes it capable of analyzing long documents and large codebases.

The model officially supports 12 languages, including English, French, Japanese, Arabic, Spanish, and Chinese.

Getting Started With the API

Granite 4.2 8B is hosted on DeepInfra, with an OpenAI-compatible interface for integration into existing workflows.

Authentication

The API requires a DeepInfra API key. Include it in the HTTP Authorization header as a bearer token:

Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_DEEPINFRA_API_KEY>

Content-Type: application/json

API Endpoint Basics

  • Base URL: https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai
  • Path: /chat/completions
  • Model Identifier: ibm-granite/granite-4.2-8b

cURL Example

curl -X POST "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions" \

  -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPINFRA_API_KEY" \

  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \

  -d '{

    "model": "ibm-granite/granite-4.2-8b",

    "messages": [

      {"role": "user", "content": "Solve: If a store sells 12 pens for $18, how much do 30 pens cost?"}

    ],

    "temperature": 0.7

  }'copy

Python Example

import os

import requests

api_key = os.environ.get("DEEPINFRA_API_KEY")

url = "https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai/chat/completions"

payload = {

    "model": "ibm-granite/granite-4.2-8b",

    "messages": [

        {"role": "system", "content": "Be a helpful assistant."},

        {"role": "user", "content": "Write a Python function to check if a string is a palindrome."}

    ],

    "temperature": 0.7,

    "max_tokens": 1024

}

response = requests.post(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}, json=payload)

print(response.json())copy

Configuration and Parameters

The API supports the following parameters to fine-tune model behavior:

ParameterTypeDefaultDescription
max_tokensintegernot setMaximum new tokens to generate, capped by the model’s context length
temperaturefloat1Controls randomness (0 is deterministic, higher is more creative)
top_pfloat1Nucleus sampling probability cutoff
repetition_penaltyfloat1Discourages repetitive text generation
stoparraynot setSequences that halt token generation
response_formatobjecttextSet to json_object or json_schema for structured JSON output
tools / tool_choicearray / stringnot setDefines callable functions and controls tool invocation
prompt_cache_keystringnot setExplicit key for reusing cached prompt state across requests

The tools / tool_choice parameters are what make tool calling work: the model decides which function to invoke and supplies arguments that match its schema.

The response_format parameter is how you request reliable structured data output instead of free-form text.

Response Format

Because Granite 4.2 8B is a reasoning model, the content field in the response includes the reasoning steps followed by the final answer:

{

  "choices": [

    {

      "message": {

        "role": "assistant",

        "content": "<think>\n12 pens cost $18, so 1 pen is $1.50. 30 * $1.50 = $45.\n</think>\n30 pens will cost $45."

      }

    }

  ]

}copy

Pricing and Usage

DeepInfra prices Granite 4.2 8B on a per-token basis:

  • Input tokens: $0.06 per 1 million tokens
  • Output tokens: $0.25 per 1 million tokens
  • Prompt caching: $0.015 per 1 million cached tokens, which reduces costs for repeated system prompts or large context windows

Private endpoint deployments and dedicated hosting are available for high-volume enterprise needs.

Technical Background

Granite 4.2 8B was post-trained from Granite 4.1 8B Base using a three-stage pipeline. The final stage used Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement learning technique, run on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster.

This training supports what IBM calls reasoning-augmented tool calling, where the model reasons about which tool to use and why it fits the task.

Related Models on DeepInfra

Granite 4.2 8B sits alongside other efficient models on DeepInfra that handle tool calling and agentic workloads:

  • Gemma 4 26B A4B IT: a mixture-of-experts model with 25.2B total and 3.8B active parameters. It offers a 262,144-token context window and supports JSON output, function calling, and multimodal input
  • Qwen3.6-35B-A3B: a multimodal mixture-of-experts model with 35B total and 3B active parameters and a native 262,144-token context window
  • GLM-5.3-Flash: a natively multimodal model with a 1,048,576-token context window and support for JSON output and function calling
  • DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731: a model with a 1,048,576-token context window and support for JSON output and function calling

Conclusion

Granite 4.2 8B bridges lightweight efficiency and deep logical processing. Its native chain-of-thought, large context window, and flexible thinking modes make it a fit for agentic workflows and enterprise coding tasks.

Key takeaways:

  • Reasoning: strong scores on AIME 2025 and SWE-Bench Verified
  • Flexibility: toggle between full reasoning and low-latency modes
  • Cost: usage-based pricing with prompt caching discounts

Get an API key and try Granite 4.2 8B on DeepInfra.

item.title: [DeepInfra] Wan 3.0 API Benchmarks: Speed, Latency & Cost
item.content:encoded:
Wan 3.0 API Benchmarks: Speed, Latency & Cost

Published on 2026.10.21 by DeepInfra

Key Takeaways

  • Wan 3.0 leads the Artificial Analysis text-to-video leaderboard with audio at 1,173 Elo, so provider choice comes down to price, input support, and reliability.
  • Per-second prices vary widely. Alibaba Cloud and fal list $0.05, $0.10, and $0.20 at 480P, 720P, and 1080P, and OpenRouter lists a rate from $0.0425.
  • DeepInfra lists one rate of $0.20 per second, serves the whole Wan family from Wan2.2 to Wan3.0 through one API, and applies a zero-retention policy.
  • OpenRouter publishes measured latency and availability for Wan 3.0, which makes operational risk easier to price in.

Wan is Alibaba’s family of video generation models. The earlier Wan2.2 models ship as open weights under Apache 2.0, while later releases such as Wan2.6, Wan2.7, and Wan3.0 are delivered through hosted APIs.

Wan 3.0 is the first Wan model to accept documents and web pages as input. It also doubles the maximum clip length to 30 seconds.

ModelKey capabilitiesAccess
Wan 3.0Clips up to 30 seconds, 480P to 1080P, native audio, document and web page inputHosted API
Wan 2.7Clips up to 15 seconds, image-to-video, reference-to-video, video editingHosted API
Wan 2.6Multi-shot storytelling, consistent subjects, clips up to 15 secondsHosted API
Wan 2.2Open-weight text-to-video and image-to-video modelsOpen weights (Apache 2.0)

On the Artificial Analysis text-to-video leaderboard with audio, Wan 3.0 ranks first at 1,173 Elo. Utopai X follows at 1,166, then Dreamina Seedance 2.5 at 1,159 and MiniMax H3 at 1,158. The 95% interval for Wan 3.0 runs from 1,157 to 1,189, so the top models sit close together.

Provider Comparison Table

The table lists the standard Wan 3.0 tier. Prices are per second of generated video.

Provider480P720P1080PNotes
DeepInfra$0.20$0.20$0.20Single listed rate
Alibaba Cloud (Singapore)$0.05$0.10$0.20US and Europe regions list $0.041256, $0.082513, and $0.165025
OpenRouter$0.0425$0.085$0.17Includes a 15% discount, one provider behind the endpoint
fal$0.05$0.10$0.20Prime tier also available
Atlas Cloud$0.04Not listed$0.16Includes a 20% discount shown on the page

How the Providers Are Compared

  • Price per second: The listed rate at each resolution tier, since video models bill by generated duration.
  • Input support: Whether the endpoint accepts reference images, video, audio, documents, and web pages.
  • Operational data: Latency and availability where a provider publishes them.
  • Data handling: Retention policy and compliance certifications.
  • Quality: Artificial Analysis scores Wan 3.0 as a model, which keeps the focus on the four factors above.

Top API Providers for Wan Models

DeepInfra

DeepInfra serves the Wan family from Wan2.2 through Wan3.0 behind one API, so teams can move between generations without changing vendors. Wan3.0-Video is billed at $0.20 per second of output.

The Wan models available on DeepInfra are:

ModelPriceCapabilities
Wan3.0-Video$0.20 per secondClips up to 30 seconds, omni-modal reference, audio
Wan2.7-R2V$0.10 per secondReference-to-video that keeps the look and voice of people or objects
Wan2.6-T2V$0.10 per secondText-to-video with multi-shot storytelling, up to 15 seconds
Wan2.2-T2V-A14B$0.075 per secondOpen-weight text-to-video model at 480p

DeepInfra also lists Wan2.7-I2V and Wan2.6-I2V at $0.10 per second. Artificial Analysis includes the Wan 2.2 A14B endpoint on DeepInfra in its generation-time tracking.

Data handling is a strength. DeepInfra runs a zero-retention policy for inputs, outputs, and user data, and the platform is SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certified.

The trade-off is price at low resolutions. The single $0.20 rate matches Alibaba Cloud’s 1080P price but sits above the 480P and 720P rates elsewhere.

Verdict: DeepInfra fits teams that render final clips at 1080P, want one API across several Wan generations, and need clear data handling terms.

Alibaba Cloud

Alibaba Cloud offers direct access through Model Studio, with the full Wan 3.0 feature set and regional pricing. The Singapore region lists $0.05, $0.10, and $0.20 per second. Regions in the US, Germany, Japan, and China list $0.041256, $0.082513, and $0.165025.

  • Rate limit of 300 requests per minute in every listed region
  • A Prime tier at $0.068, $0.14, and $0.28 per second in Singapore, aimed at faster generation
  • Editing, extension, and reference-guided generation from the first-party API
  • No support for batch inference or fine-tuning

Alibaba notes that audio texture and on-screen text rendering are still maturing. Verdict: Alibaba Cloud suits enterprise teams that want first-party access and regional pricing options.

OpenRouter

OpenRouter lists Wan 3.0 under alibaba/wan-3.0 with a release date of August 24, 2026. It routes to a single provider, Alibaba Cloud, and shows rates from $0.0425 per second at 480P with a 15% discount applied.

OpenRouter publishes operational data for the endpoint. At the time of writing, the best provider shows a median end-to-end latency of about 149 seconds and availability near 85% over three days. These figures move, so check the live page.

Verdict: OpenRouter fits cost-sensitive teams that want one billing relationship and visible reliability data.

fal

fal serves Wan 3.0 through the alibaba/wan-3.0 endpoints and lists $0.05, $0.10, and $0.20 per second at 480p, 720p, and 1080p. A Prime variant lists $0.068, $0.14, and $0.28.

  • Duration from 2 to 30 seconds, with a null value for smart duration
  • Aspect ratios of adaptive, 16:9, 4:3, 1:1, 3:4, and 9:16
  • A JavaScript client published as @fal-ai/client
  • A safety checker that is on by default

Turning off prompt expansion can save roughly 20 to 60 seconds of latency, according to fal. Verdict: fal fits web teams that want a typed client and queue-based requests.

Atlas Cloud

Atlas Cloud lists Wan 3.0 at $0.05 per second, shown as $0.04 after a 20% discount. A Prime tier lists $0.068, shown as $0.061 after 10% off. The page lists SOC 2 Type II certification and HIPAA alignment.

Reference-to-video accepts up to 20 mixed references: 10 images, 5 videos, and 5 audio clips. Verdict: Atlas Cloud suits teams with compliance requirements that also want low per-second rates.

Why DeepInfra Fits Production Wan Workloads

Price per second is only one input. Production teams also weigh data handling, vendor count, and how easily they can add other models later.

  • One API covers every Wan generation from Wan2.2 to Wan3.0, plus other video models such as Google Veo 3.1 Fast at $0.15 per second.
  • Zero retention and SOC 2 and ISO 27001 certification cover regulated review processes.
  • A single listed rate makes budgeting simple for fixed-resolution pipelines.

The table shows what a 10-second clip costs at each resolution. DeepInfra’s single rate makes it a fit for 1080P work.

Provider480P720P1080P
DeepInfra$2.00$2.00$2.00
Alibaba Cloud (Singapore)$0.50$1.00$2.00
OpenRouter$0.425$0.85$1.70
fal$0.50$1.00$2.00

Teams that also run video models from other labs can add Google Veo 3.1 Fast through the same API.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which provider is cheapest for Wan 3.0?

It depends on resolution. At 480P, Atlas Cloud shows $0.04 after its discount, Alibaba’s US region lists $0.041256, and OpenRouter lists $0.0425. At 1080P, Atlas Cloud shows $0.16 and OpenRouter lists $0.17.

How much does a Wan 3.0 video cost through an API?

A 5-second 720P clip costs about $0.425 on OpenRouter, $0.50 on Alibaba Cloud’s Singapore region and fal, and $1.00 on DeepInfra. A 5-second 1080P clip costs $1.00 on DeepInfra, Alibaba Cloud, and fal.

What is the difference between Wan 2.x and Wan 3.0?

Wan 3.0 extends a single generation to 30 seconds, up from 15 seconds in Wan 2.7. It adds document and web page input, carries forward the editing features from Wan 2.7, and ships as a managed service.

Is Wan 3.0 open source?

Alibaba offers Wan 3.0 through managed APIs. The Wan2.2 weights are published on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license.

Can I run Wan locally?

Yes, with Wan2.2. The Wan2.2 T2V A14B and TI2V 5B weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. DeepInfra also hosts the A14B model if you prefer an API.

Conclusion

Choosing a Wan API provider means comparing price at your working resolution, the inputs you need, and how much operational data the provider publishes. Quality is set by the model, so the decision rests on those practical factors.

  • Choose DeepInfra for one API across Wan generations, 1080P final renders, and zero-retention data handling.
  • Choose Alibaba Cloud for first-party access, regional pricing, and a Prime tier.
  • Choose OpenRouter for a low 1080P rate and published reliability figures.
  • Choose fal or Atlas Cloud for a typed client or compliance listings.

A similar comparison for language models covers GLM-5.3 API providers.

You may need to repeat much of that work when another AI […]</p>

Three of the strongest models available on DeepInfra right now don’t separate cleanly by capability tier. Kimi K3 (available via DeepInfra), Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.6 Sol all score within […]</p>

item.content:encoded:
From Search Results to Evidence: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank on DeepInfra

Published on 2026.10.21 by Aray Sultanbekova

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank, part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever collection, are available on DeepInfra from Day 0. Starting today, you can access Embed 1B, Embed 8B, and Rerank 8B through the DeepInfra API with no deployment setup and pay-per-token pricing.

Enterprise agents are only as good as the information they can retrieve. A support agent needs the specific clause from a policy PDF. A finance agent needs the number contained in a chart, rather than the surrounding text.

Traditional text-only retrieval can miss critical information embedded in tables, charts, and complex document layouts. Nemotron 3.5 Embed helps retrieve information across text and visual content, while Rerank prioritizes the most relevant results for downstream reasoning.

Together, they help developers build retrieval pipelines that provide agents with stronger evidence while using their context and inference budgets more efficiently.

What’s new in Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank?

Embed and Rerank are part of NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever, a collection of open, leaderboard-winning models for building retrieval systems for agents, alongside Nemotron 3.5 Parse for turning complex documents into structured, agent-ready content.

Multimodal embeddings. Nemotron 3.5 Embed creates unified representations across text, tables, charts, images, diagrams, and document pages, so agents can retrieve information even when the answer is expressed visually. It comes in two sizes: 1B for efficiency at scale and 8B for quality-focused retrieval, particularly in agentic workflows.

Reranking built for agents. Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B scores retrieved passages against an agent’s question, then prioritizes the most relevant evidence for the reasoning model. It supports agents that retrieve iteratively and compare evidence across multiple sources.

Better retrieval quality, more efficient agent workflows. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B leads the ViDoRe v3.1 leaderboard among dense retrieval models, while adding Nemotron 3.5 Rerank reduces agent inference costs by up to 14% in NVIDIA evaluations.

Open and customizable. The weights are open, and NVIDIA publishes NeMo post-training recipes for adapting retrieval to your own terminology, data, and relevance criteria.

What you can build

  • Agentic RAG over enterprise documents: Retrieve relevant information from PDFs, presentations, scanned pages, tables, charts, and diagrams—not just extracted text.
  • Multi-step research agents: Support query rewriting, iterative retrieval, and evidence comparison across multiple resources.
  • Agent memory and code retrieval: Retrieve relevant context from stored interactions, technical documentation, and code repositories to support long-running workflows and coding agents.

Getting started on DeepInfra

Get an API key from the DeepInfra dashboard and set it as DEEPINFRA_TOKEN. The example below embeds a support question and four passages with Embed 1B, keeps the three closest, and reranks them with Rerank 8B. Set input_type to "query" for questions and "passage" for the content you search over.

import os

import numpy as np
import requests
from openai import OpenAI

TOKEN = os.environ["DEEPINFRA_TOKEN"]
EMBED = "nvidia/Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16"
RERANK = "nvidia/Nemotron-3.5-Rerank-8B-BF16"

client = OpenAI(
    api_key=TOKEN,
    base_url="https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/openai",
)

query = "What is the refund window for annual plans?"
docs = [
    "Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time from the billing page.",
    "Annual plans can be refunded in full within 30 days of purchase.",
    "Enterprise contracts follow the terms in the signed order form.",
    "Invoices are emailed on the first business day of each month.",
]

# 1. Retrieve: embed the query and documents, keep the closest matches
q = client.embeddings.create(
    model=EMBED, input=[query], extra_body={"input_type": "query"}
)
d = client.embeddings.create(
    model=EMBED, input=docs, extra_body={"input_type": "passage"}
)
q_vec = np.array(q.data[0].embedding)
d_vecs = np.array([e.embedding for e in d.data])
similarity = d_vecs @ q_vec  # vectors are L2-normalized
candidates = [docs[i] for i in np.argsort(-similarity)[:3]]

# 2. Rerank: score each candidate against the query
resp = requests.post(
    f"https://api.deepinfra.com/v1/inference/{RERANK}",
    headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"},
    json={"queries": [query] * len(candidates), "documents": candidates},
)
for score, doc in sorted(zip(resp.json()["scores"], candidates), reverse=True):
    print(f"{score:.3f}  {doc}")
copy

Output:

-1.112  Annual plans can be refunded in full within 30 days of purchase.
-2.912  Monthly plans can be cancelled at any time from the billing page.
-3.290  Invoices are emailed on the first business day of each month.
copy

The passage that answers the question comes out on top. Rerank returns raw relevance scores, so negative values are expected.

Tip: search page images, too. Embed also accepts images, so a screenshot of a policy table can be retrieved by a plain-language question:

import base64

with open("refund_policy_page.png", "rb") as f:
    page_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

page = client.embeddings.create(
    model=EMBED,
    input=[[
        {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{page_b64}"}},
    ]],
    extra_body={"input_type": "passage"},
)
page_vec = np.array(page.data[0].embedding)
print(f"{page_vec @ q_vec:.3f}")
copy

Output: 0.576 (vs. 0.110 for "How do I reset my password?")

Pricing

DeepInfra offers pay-per-token access to Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B, Embed 8B, and Rerank 8B. Per 1M input tokens, each with a 32K-token context window:

  • Embed 1B is $0.015 for text, $0.035 for image inputs
  • Embed 8B is $0.035 for text, $0.070 for image inputs
  • Rerank 8B is $0.050

See DeepInfra pricing for current rates.

item.title: [xAI Grok] Using Grok Bot to detect and respond to incidents
item.content:encoded:
Back to newsOct 20, 2026

Using Grok Bot to detect and respond to incidents

By Chris Bowie and Isaac Hopkinson

IncidentWatch spots ticket spikes before internal alerts fire. IncidentSweep clears the related backlog in an approved batch.

Download for macOSContact sales

When a product incident occurs, the support queue can be one of the first places it shows up. Customers start reporting the same issue, sometimes before engineering alerts fire or anyone has declared an incident.

Those reports keep coming while the incident unfolds. At first, support may not know what is wrong or have an answer we can confidently provide. By the time the issue is resolved, hundreds or thousands of customers may be waiting for a response. Support has to track those customers through the incident, then make sure each gets the right answer when it is resolved.

We use Grok Bot to handle both parts of this work. It provides us with AI teammates that take ownership of operational jobs, particularly repetitive workflows that otherwise fall between people and systems. As we shared in a recent blog, the SpaceXSI customer support team uses Support Bot in Grok Bot to handle customer-facing communication.

Now we’ve added two more AI teammates that we call on specifically for incidents. The first, IncidentWatch, monitors the support queue for spikes in similar tickets and alerts our team when it sees one. The second, IncidentSweep, handles the other end, identifying affected tickets and closing them in an approved batch.

During one incident on September 18, our Bot, IncidentSweep, cleared 204 tickets in about 10 minutes with a support engineer reviewing and approving the batch. Previously, we would have had to reply to those tickets one by one over the course of hours or use a bulk macro that gave us much less control over who received the message.

Detecting incidents through customer reports

Customers often notice problems before our internal alerts fire. When several customers report the same issue at once, those tickets can be an early signal of an incident.

IncidentWatch is a Grok Bot teammate we built to detect that signal. Every five minutes, it reviews the previous 15 minutes of tickets for spikes around the same problem. If the pattern does not match a known incident, IncidentWatch alerts the support engineer on call with the apparent issue, number of matching tickets, and examples to investigate.

A support engineer decides whether the reports point to an incident and works with engineering to investigate. In the meantime, IncidentWatch holds tickets that clearly match the issue.

Once the team confirms the incident, we post it to our public status page. Support Bot, our primary customer-facing Bot, returns to the held tickets, checks them against the incident, and responds to customers whose reports match. As the incident progresses, it can return with updates.

Clearing the incident backlog

Once an incident is resolved, there may still be hundreds of related tickets in the queue, and each needs a final response. Traditionally, support teams have had two ways to clear them, and both have drawbacks. They can respond to each ticket individually, which can take hours, or use a bulk action, which is fast but leaves little room to catch a ticket that should not receive the message.

We built IncidentSweep to combine the control of the first approach with the speed of the second.

A support engineer starts by telling IncidentSweep which tickets to consider, which to exclude, and exactly what message to send. IncidentSweep finds the matching tickets, reviews each one, and sets aside any it cannot confidently connect to the incident.

Before sending anything, IncidentSweep shows the engineer the proposed batch, the tickets it included, and the exact message they will receive. The engineer can spot-check the tickets and make changes before approving the send.

IncidentSweep then sends the approved message in small batches and records each action. It never adds tickets after approval, and if anything fails, it stops and reports what happened.

Give Bots jobs, not tasks

Grok Bot introduces a different way of working with AI. Instead of turning to an AI tool for help with individual tasks, teams can create AI teammates that own jobs and carry entire workflows through to an outcome.

Customer support has been a natural place for us to put this model to work. IncidentWatch and IncidentSweep take on jobs that used to require someone on the team to watch, sort, and act on hundreds of individual tickets. Across SpaceXSI, we’re looking for more workflows where AI teammates can take on the same kind of ownership.

Try Grok Bot today

Thinking

Summary

Voxtral 3 introduces a cutting-edge voice agent SDK and state-of-the-art speech models designed for real-time, multi-step conversations across 50+ languages. It combines accurate transcription, natural speech synthesis with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration for seamless workflow automation. Available via Mistral’s EU-hosted API or self-deployment, it ensures data sovereignty while delivering low-latency, human-like interactions for contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.

Speech transcription and voice generation have come a long way, but building end-to-end voice agents that can listen, reason, interact, and handle complex workflows remains difficult.

A reliable voice agent needs to do four things very well (and simultaneously):

  • Listen accurately across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions,
  • Reason deeply about what users mean in specific contexts,
  • Speak naturally with emotion and expression, and
  • Take action over multiple steps through connected systems.

Getting all four to work together reliably in real time remains a challenge.

To address this, we introduce Voxtral 3: a new family of state-of-the-art speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, alongside a voice agent SDK that brings listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into a single real-time streaming pipeline.

Voxtral 3 is built to create natural conversational experiences, from contact-center agents and service desks to virtual assistants and hands-free copilots. With support for dozens of languages, expressive speech, complex reasoning, and deep integration with your own tools and data, agents built with Voxtral can interpret nuanced intent, reason through sophisticated requests, and execute multi-step actions across connected systems.

As with other Mistral models, the Voxtral 3 family is designed for sovereign deployment. Available today through Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment on your own infrastructure, it gives organizations control over where audio is processed, how data is handled, and whether conversations are retained.

Highlights

  • Accurate transcription across 50+ languages. The speech-to-text model, Voxtral Small Transcribe 3, is state-of-the-art in multilingual transcription, identifying who said what (diarization), using keyphrases to improve its accuracy (context-biasing). It detects when someone has finished speaking so agents can respond without delay (end-of-turn detection).
  • Natural speech that adapts to the conversation. The text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3, introduces new voices that adjust their emotion, pace, and emphasis based on conversational context, with support for 35+ languages and 50+ dialects.
  • Human-like intelligence at your (spoken) command. The new voice agent SDK combines listening, reasoning, tool calling, and speaking into a real-time experience. Agents can retrieve information, interact with business systems, and complete tasks during live conversations over phone or web.
  • Pro Voice for distinctly accurate voice adaptation. For professional use cases where basic voice cloning does not suffice, Voxtral’s Pro Voice adaptation is able to reproduce a speaker’s distinctive character, emotional range, and speaking style across languages, using just 30 minutes of audio.
  • Your voice AI, on your infrastructure. Use Mistral's EU-hosted API or deploy Voxtral 3 on your own infrastructure. Keep sensitive conversations within your environment and control whether any audio is retained.

Try Voxtral now | Learn more

It hears 50+ languages, with state-of-the-art accuracy.

Voxtral Transcribe 3 represents a significant milestone across transcription, diarization (who spoke when) and context biasing capabilities. The supported list of languages is expanded to 50, including 24 official EU languages and many low-resource Asian and Indic languages.

The Small version achieves state-of-the-art results across diarization and multilingual transcription, including in English, French and Spanish. It outperforms Whisper, Scribe v2 and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. The Mini variant is 4B parameters, enabling fast and accurate transcriptions at a price of $0.0035/min.

Both models support context biasing, where key terms and free-form text can be given to bias the transcription and improve recall on technical terms. This enables them to be used in production settings with domain-specific vocabulary without the need for fine-tuning.

End-of-turn prediction is natively supported, incorporating both acoustic and semantic information to accurately predict when a user is finished speaking. This allows for low-latency voice agent applications, while minimizing false cut-off rates when the user is prematurely interrupted.

The speech model implicitly interprets the semantic meaning of context better, producing natural speech across a diverse range of emotions and languages. The voice agent is in control of the whole conversation.

Voxtral 3 introduces a voice agent SDK, built on LiveKit, that runs speech in, reasoning, and speech out as one streaming pipeline. Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 listens and detects when the caller has finished speaking, a general model—like Mistral Small—reasons and calls tools, and Voxtral Speech 3 replies in the tone of the conversation so far. No stage waits for the one before it, so each turn completes in under one second, and the agent stops talking when the caller cuts in.

During a call, the agent can verify a caller's identity, check a bill, or book an appointment, using function calling, web search, and retrieval over your own systems. It answers and places calls over SIP, runs in browsers and apps over WebRTC, and connects to the telephony, IVR, and contact-center software you already use.

Each stage is a separate model, so you can change the LLM, the voice, or the language without rewriting the agent, and run the whole stack on Mistral's API in Europe or on your own infrastructure.

item.title: [Cohere] Rethinking confidence in reasoning models
item.content:encoded:
Oct 20, 2026

6 minute read

Rethinking confidence in reasoning models

You roll two fair six-sided dice. What is the probability that their sum is at least 10?

A model might hesitate at first. Then it counts the possibilities: three ways to roll 10, two ways to roll 11, and one way to roll 12. Six outcomes out of 36. The answer is 1/6.

In our illustrative example (figure below, on the left), the model starts at 25% confidence and finishes at 88%. Those percentages describe its confidence in getting the answer right, not the probability of the dice outcome. Working through the problem has changed its assessment.

Confidence can move the other way, too (figure below, on the right). Reasoning through a solution that initially looks straightforward may reveal a mistaken assumption or a contradiction. A useful confidence estimate should be able to reflect that change, even when the model still gives the wrong answer. However, standard reasoning models do not necessarily come with this ability: producing a detailed reasoning process does not guarantee that a model can reliably assess and communicate its uncertainty.

This is the idea behind our method CALIBER: train a reasoning model to estimate its chance of success before it begins, then assess its particular answer afterwards. On our math benchmark, the calibrated 7B model reduces calibration error by more than half compared with the best single-confidence baseline on this metriic. The key is that the two confidence estimates answer different questions.

One confidence score hides two questions

Before reasoning, the model has only seen the question. It can recognise the topic and judge whether the problem looks manageable. Its confidence answers: “How likely am I to solve this?”

After reasoning, it has something more specific to assess: the solution it actually produced. Now the question is: “How likely is this answer to be correct?”

These predictions are related, but they serve different purposes. Initial confidence gives an indication of whether the model expects to handle the question successfully. Final confidence helps a user judge whether the resulting answer needs closer scrutiny. A model might often solve this kind of problem and still make a mistake on this attempt. Or it might approach a difficult question cautiously, then find a solution it can check.

CALIBER trains the model to report both estimates in one response: initial confidence, reasoning, an answer, and final confidence. The two numbers can disagree because reasoning gives the model new information to assess. The goal is to make these estimates meaningful enough to support decisions about when to accept an answer, verify it, or seek help.

Teaching confidence what to predict

To train initial confidence, we let the model try the same question several times. If seven out of ten attempts succeed, 70% becomes the training target. That captures how often the current model can solve the question, before we know which particular attempt it will produce.

Final confidence gets a different target: whether that individual answer is correct. A successful and an unsuccessful attempt at the same question share an initial-confidence target, but receive different final-confidence targets. The figure below shows how this works.

In this example, three of four attempts succeed, giving an initial-confidence target of 75%. The fourth attempt produces a wrong answer, so its final-confidence target is 0. The displayed 60% and 20% are the model’s predictions. Training rewards it for moving those predictions closer to their respective targets.

We combine these confidence rewards with a reward for answering correctly. The model is encouraged both to solve the problem and to assess its chances accurately. Recognizing uncertainty about a wrong answer can improve its confidence reward, but it does not earn the reward for a correct solution. The aim is to make confidence more useful while keeping the model focused on getting the answer right.

Why saying 70 percent every time is not enough

Imagine a model that answers 70% of questions correctly and reports 70% confidence every time. Its confidence matches its overall accuracy perfectly. But if you only have time to check a few answers, those identical scores give you no way to choose.

Now imagine another model with the same overall accuracy. It assigns 90% confidence to half its answers and 50% to the other half. If those groups are correct 90% and 50% of the time, respectively, this model is also calibrated. Its confidence is more useful, though: it helps you focus your checks on the answers more likely to contain mistakes.

We therefore evaluate two properties together. Expected Calibration Error (ECE) measures whether confidence matches observed accuracy: among answers assigned roughly 80% confidence, roughly 80% should be correct. AUROC measures whether correct answers tend to receive higher confidence than incorrect ones. Lower ECE and higher AUROC are better. Together, they show whether the confidence values are reliable and whether they help identify likely errors.

The figure illustrates these complementary goals: confidence should match observed accuracy and help distinguish correct answers from mistakes.

Better confidence on math and beyond

We trained 7B and 30B models on 30,000 math problems and evaluated them on 1,000 held-out problems, plus three question-answering benchmarks. Our comparisons use a shared training setup; the “lite” baselines are simplified adaptations of earlier methods. For CALIBER, the reported calibration metrics evaluate final confidence.

On BigMathDigits, the 7B model’s ECE falls from 0.059 for the strongest single-confidence baseline to 0.028 for CALIBER – a 52.5% reduction. CALIBER also achieves the best AUROC (0.806) and Brier score (0.130), showing improvements both in how closely confidence matches accuracy and in how well it distinguishes correct answers from mistakes.

The improvements extend beyond math. Without further training or task-specific checkpoint selection, the 7B model reduces calibration error by 26.8% on GPQA, 32.2% on TriviaQA, and 36.2% on SimpleQA, compared with the strongest single-confidence baseline on each dataset.

The 30B results show why the metrics matter together. On BigMathDigits, CALIBER’s ECE of 0.022 is only slightly better than CoCA-lite’s 0.023. But its AUROC is 0.797, compared with 0.508 for CoCA-lite: a large difference in how well confidence distinguishes correct from incorrect answers. Other baselines achieve slightly higher AUROC than CALIBER, so the benefit depends on which property we measure.

Confidence versus observed accuracy on BigMathDigits for the 30B model. Curves closer to the diagonal are better calibrated.

What a change in confidence tells us

Having two estimates lets us see whether the model revises its assessment after reasoning. On BigMathDigits, the 7B model’s mean confidence rises from 78.5% to 83.5% for correct answers and falls from 62.6% to 54.5% for incorrect answers. On other datasets, it sometimes lowers confidence for both groups, with a larger decrease for incorrect answers.

A rise or fall is therefore context, not a verdict. Two answers that finish at 70% confidence express the same estimated probability of correctness, even if one estimate rose and the other fell. The final estimate assesses the answer; the change tells us how the model’s assessment evolved.

Our experiments take this measurement before and after a single reasoning process. A next question is whether reliable confidence updates could help a model decide when to verify, retrieve more information, or abstain. We have not tested those uses here. CALIBER provides a starting point: confidence trained to reflect what the model can assess at each stage of reasoning.

Read the paper for the full experimental setup and results: CALIBER.

item.title: [Hugging Face] Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

Published October 20, 2026

Update on GitHub

10

Alvaro Moran

tengomucho

Jingya Huang

Jingya

Simon Pagezy

pagezyhf

Jeff Boudier

jeffboudier

Régis Pierrard

regisss

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

The old way

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

Enter TorchTPU 🚀

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Your favourite libraries, now on TPU

Transformers

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline

pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained(
    "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium", dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipe.to("tpu")  # eager mode: that's the whole change
# optional: compiled mode
pipe.transformer.compile(backend="tpu", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)

image = pipe("a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon").images[0]

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

MiniMax-H3 (video + audio)Qwen-Image-2.1
"The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager"A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager"A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps

Kernels

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

from kernels import get_kernel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS

repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu"
kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507",
    experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot",
)

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We test it so you don't have to 🧪

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard]](https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard%5D).

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

Get started

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

  • TorchTPU on GitHub
  • TPU kernels on the Hub
  • Cloud TPU documentation

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

item.description: Full title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Published October 20, 2026

Update on GitHub

4

Mattt

mattt

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:

A drop-in compatible API

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

- import FoundationModels
+ import AnyLanguageModel

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

  • Tool calling works with every provider.
  • Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them.
  • Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Hosted models, too

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

  • OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs
  • Open Responses, for any provider with a compatible endpoint
  • Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options
  • Google's Gemini API
  • Ollama
  • Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27
  • Hugging Face Inference Providers, and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

let model = OpenAILanguageModel(
    baseURL: URL(string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/")!,
    apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["HF_TOKEN"]!,
    model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b",
    apiVariant: .chatCompletions
)

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Open-weight models got better

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

  • Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training.
  • LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M.
  • Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

let model = MLXLanguageModel(modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit")

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

Upgrading to 1.0

dependencies: [
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel",
        from: "1.0.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    )
]

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

What's next

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

item.title: [Hugging Face] MPS in PyTorch 2.15
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

MPS in PyTorch 2.15

Published October 20, 2026

Update on GitHub

10

Irakli Salia

Isalia20

Khushi Agrawal

khushi-411

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

TL;DR

  • FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
  • MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
  • Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
  • More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
  • Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
  • More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
  • Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
  • A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.

What this means for you

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

  • Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
  • Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
  • Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
  • FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)

Contents

  • Getting started
  • FP8 comes to MPS
  • Faster language-model decoding
  • Linear algebra gets a boost
  • Convolutions, padding, and training
  • Softmax and reductions
  • A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding
  • More control with MPS streams
  • More operations work on MPS
  • A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16
  • Wrapping up

Getting started

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu

FP8 comes to MPS

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

def quantize_fp8(x):
    limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
    scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
    return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale

x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)

y = F.scaled_mm(
    x_fp8,
    w_fp8.t(),
    scale_a=x_scale,
    scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    scale_b=w_scale,
    scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
    output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)

Faster language-model decoding

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

Linear layers

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

Mixture-of-experts layers

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)

out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape)  # torch.Size([64, 128])

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Linear algebra gets a boost

Complex-valued computations

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

import torch

a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)

lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())

Small matrices and larger solves

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Convolutions, padding, and training

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

OperationWhat changes in 2.15
conv1d forwardSpecialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes.
Constant paddingMoves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below).
Reflection and replication paddingNew Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness.
Out-of-place dropoutnn.Dropout and F.dropout now use the existing fused kernel.
Upsampling backwardA Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path.
Channels-last conv2d backwardStays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access.

Softmax and reductions

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

Memory metricMPSGraph paddingMetal padding
Current tensor-allocation peak4.422 GiB4.095 GiB
Allocator-reserved peak8.070 GiB8.070 GiB
Total driver-memory peak270.135 GiB8.108 GiB

More control with MPS streams

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

import torch

x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()

with torch.mps.stream(worker):
    y = x.square()
    x.record_stream(worker)

del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)

More operations work on MPS

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Faster LLM decoding

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

ModelBeforeAfterChange
LFM2.5-8B-A1B108.8 tokens/s126.0 tokens/s+16%
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B52.9 tokens/s62.8 tokens/s+19%
Qwen3.8-27B12.1 tokens/s12.6 tokens/s+4%

Attention runs entirely on Metal

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

More MPSGraph to Metal migrations

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

A smaller install

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

Wrapping up

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

What's next for us

  • More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
  • torch.compile: we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.
  • Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know.

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.
